subject: Safeguarding Training of Trainers
title: Safeguarding Training of Trainers and Capacity Building (6-Week Course)
tagline: Build a safe organisation and train others: policies, culture, roles, risk assessment, safer recruitment, reporting, response, media and awareness. Starts with a full table of contents.

units.title: Welcome: Course Map and Table of Contents
units.summary: See the whole course at a glance: what you will learn each week, how each unit is built, how you will be assessed and how to get the most from the training.

p: This course teaches you how to keep children and adults safe from harm caused by an organisation's own people and activities. It also teaches you how to train others to do the same. That is why it is called a Training of Trainers (ToT) and capacity building course.

It is written in simple words. You do not need to know the law or to have worked in safeguarding before. If you are a teacher, a school leader, a programme officer, a volunteer coordinator or a community worker, this course is for you.
What you will be able to do at the end:
• Explain what safeguarding is and what it is not.
• Spot abuse, power imbalances and safeguarding risks in real situations.
• Explain the main laws that protect children in Nigeria and Lagos.
• Check a safeguarding policy and turn it into working procedures.
• Build a safeguarding culture in your school or organisation.
• Carry out a safeguarding risk assessment, score the risks and escalate them.
• Recruit and induct staff and volunteers safely.
• Set up reporting channels that people will use, and respond well to a disclosure.
• Plan, teach and follow up a safeguarding awareness session for others.

b: Teachers, school heads and school safeguarding leads.
Programme staff, field officers and community volunteers.
Managers, HR officers, finance and procurement staff.
Anyone who will train colleagues, partners or communities.

How to study:

• Do the activity before you move on. Writing things down helps you remember.
• If you can, study with a colleague and compare your answers.
• Keep a notebook for your action plan. You will use it in the last unit.

b: Two or three study sessions of 60 to 90 minutes.

sections.h: What the final assessment is like
p: At the end of the course you take one assessment with 100 multiple-choice questions.
Key facts:
• The questions are difficult. They test whether you can apply what you learned, not only remember it.
• Each question has four options. The options are written to look alike, so you must think carefully.
• You need 75% to pass and earn your course certificate.
• Only the final assessment counts. The practice questions in each unit do not add to your score.
Tips:
• Read each question twice and look at every option.
• Look for words such as 'first', 'best', 'most likely' and 'not'.
• Think about the survivor's safety first. It is usually the key to the best answer.

b: Write down one safeguarding situation from your own work that you want to understand better.
Write down one thing you hope to change in your organisation.
Read your notes again at the end of the course.

units.title: What Safeguarding Is, Key Terms and the Four Pillars
units.summary: Define safeguarding and related terms, learn what safeguarding is not, and understand the four pillars: awareness, prevention, reporting and response.

p: Safeguarding is the responsibility of every organisation to make sure its staff, operations and programmes do no harm to children, adults and staff. This includes contractors, partners and representatives. It also means protecting them from abuse, exploitation and neglect.
The safeguarding question: could our people, or our activities, cause harm here?
• Child safeguarding covers everyone under 18.
• Adult safeguarding covers adults at risk, staff and community members that our work reaches.
• Safeguarding is about harm caused by us or our work. It is not only about harm that happens in families or the community.

b: A volunteer who runs a weekend class offers one girl 'extra lessons' alone at his house. This is a safeguarding concern about our own volunteer.
A child who is beaten at home is a child protection concern, and the organisation may help, but the harm was not caused by our people.

img.alt: Silhouette of a child at a window with hands on the glass
img.cap: Safeguarding means keeping every child safe, including from harm that could come from our own people.

sections.h: Key related terms: define and explain
p: Learn these terms. Each one is used in the rest of the course.
• PSEAH: Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment. The commitments, systems and actions that stop staff and representatives from sexually exploiting, abusing or harassing anyone.
• Sexual exploitation: any real or attempted abuse of a position of vulnerability, unequal power or trust for sexual purposes, including gaining money, social or political benefit.
• Sexual abuse: actual or threatened physical intrusion of a sexual nature, by force or under unequal or forced conditions.
• Sexual harassment: unwelcome sexual behaviour that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment, often between colleagues.
• Duty of care: the legal and moral duty to take reasonable steps to keep the people we work with safe from harm we can foresee.
• Do No Harm: our presence, programmes and people must never make anyone less safe than before we arrived.
• Accountability: being answerable to the people we serve, not only to donors. Communities know what to expect, can give feedback and complain, and see us act on it.

• Social safeguards: standards used by funders and development banks so that projects do not harm people or communities (labour conditions, community health and safety, and protection of vulnerable groups).
• Risk: the chance that harm happens, combined with how serious the harm would be. Safeguarding risk is about harm to people, not money or reputation.

b: Exploitation uses someone's weaker position for your own gain.
Abuse is harm done to a person, often by someone who has power over them.
Harassment is unwelcome behaviour that makes someone feel unsafe or uncomfortable at work.

p: Safeguarding overlaps with other ideas, but it is different. Being clear stops confusion.
• Safety: general physical safety such as fire exits, hard hats and preventing accidents. Safeguarding protects people from deliberate harm, abuse, exploitation and neglect by others.
• Child protection: reacts to known or suspected harm to a specific child. Safeguarding is broader and acts before harm happens, for all children and adults at risk.

• Security: protects the organisation and staff from outside threats such as theft or data breaches. Safeguarding protects beneficiaries and communities from harm caused by people inside or linked to the organisation.
• Risk management: looks at organisation risks such as money, reputation and operations. Safeguarding focuses on the risk of harm to vulnerable people.
• HR or conduct matters: staff complaints, discipline and employment issues. A safeguarding concern may start an HR process, but it is not the same thing.

• Safeguarding vs protection: safeguarding keeps people safe from harm caused by us and our work. Protection (for example child protection) responds to harm children face in their families and communities.

b: A broken fire exit is a safety issue.
A stolen laptop is a security issue.
A teacher who is hitting a pupil is a safeguarding issue.
A late payment to a vendor is a financial risk, not a safeguarding risk.

p: A strong safeguarding system rests on four pillars. If one is weak, the system is weak.
Pillar 1: Awareness. People know what safeguarding is, what harm looks like and what to do.
• Know your safeguarding policy, the signs of abuse and who the vulnerable people are in your work.
• Know your role. Communities should know their rights and how to report.
• Methods: training, induction and briefings.
Pillar 2: Prevention. Stop harm before it happens through policies, training, good practice, safe environments and safe programmes.
• Risk assessments before activities, safe programme design and a strong safeguarding culture.
• Code of conduct enforcement, safe recruitment and clear power and accountability structures.
Pillar 3: Reporting. Safe, easy ways for anyone, inside or outside the organisation, to raise a concern.
• Clear channels, several options, confidentiality, protection from retaliation and quick acknowledgement.
Pillar 4: Response. Act quickly and correctly when harm happens or is suspected.
• Survivor-centred approach, follow the policy, do not investigate alone, escalate and learn from the case.

ex.t: Self-check: where is your organisation strongest?
b: Awareness: do all staff and children know how to report?
Prevention: are risk assessments done before activities?
Reporting: can someone report without fear?
Response: does someone act within 24 hours?

units.title: Power, Vulnerability and Consent
units.summary: Understand how power creates risk, why consent is only real when a person is free to say no, and practise spotting who holds the power in real situations.

sections.h: Safeguarding is about the misuse of power
p: In every organisation some people have more power than others. People with less power are at greater risk of exploitation and abuse.
Key points:

• SEAH (sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment) happens when people inside organisations use their power harmfully against people with less power. This can be in their team, in partner organisations or in the communities they serve.
• SEAH affects women and girls most, but it also affects men and boys.
• Consent is real only when a person is free to say no. If one person controls food, pay, a job, a place to sleep or someone's safety, 'agreement' may not be free consent at all.
• Power is not fixed. Context changes who holds it.

b: A field officer registers families for support. He says to a mother, 'If you spend time with me, your name will be on the list.' Her 'yes' is not free consent.
A supervisor asks a junior staff member for a favour and holds the power to renew her contract. Her 'yes' may be fear.

img.alt: Two women talking at a table
img.cap: Whenever one person has more power than the other, take extra care.

p: Power comes from many places. Learn to name them.
• Gender, age, role and seniority.
• Employment status (permanent or temporary).
• Control of money, food or other resources.
• Education level and knowledge.
• Disability.
• Nationality or ethnicity.
• Who holds information, and who is believed.
Questions to ask when you look at any relationship:
• Who can give or take something the other person needs?
• Who would be believed if something went wrong?
• Who can leave, and who cannot?
• Who is alone, and who has witnesses?

b: The same person can have power in one setting and little power in another.
A teacher has power over pupils in school, but less power than a head teacher.
A child worker may depend on an employer for food and a bed.

p: Work in pairs. For each pair of people below, decide who has more power and why. Think about age, money, information, control of movement and who would be believed.
Scenarios:
• A: A caseworker and a 14-year-old girl who receives support. Think about access, trust and control of support.
• B: A field officer who registers families and a mother hoping to be enrolled. Think about gatekeeping, need and gender.
• C: A volunteer who runs a weekend class and the children who attend. Think about trust, authority and private contact.
• D: A driver and a child travelling to an activity. Think about being alone, no witnesses and age.
• E: A staff member taking photos for a donor report and the children in the activity. Think about consent and who decides what is shared.
• F: The Executive Director and the safeguarding focal person who must report a concern about a senior colleague. Think about seniority, job security and fear.
• G: A senior manager and a junior staff member or intern. Think about contracts, references and credibility.
• H: A child domestic worker and the employer she lives and works with. Think about dependence, control and credibility.
Then ask: does the power shift in a different setting? What could the less powerful person do if something went wrong?

ex.t: Model thinking for scenario D (driver and child)
b: Power: the driver is an adult, controls the car and the route, and may be alone with the child.
Risk: no witnesses, the child may not be believed, the child cannot leave.
Safeguards: vetted drivers, headcounts, no child alone with a driver, consent for travel.

sections.h: Activity: map where power sits in your programme
p: A power map is a simple drawing of the people in a programme and who has power over whom. It shows where harm could happen and where your safeguards must be strongest.
How to make one:
• Pick one programme, ideally one that reaches child domestic workers or other children at risk.
• Write everyone involved: children, caregivers, staff, volunteers, drivers, partners, vendors, community leaders, employers.
• Draw arrows from the person with more power to the person with less. Note where the power comes from (money, access, information, status).
• Circle the risky moments: where a less powerful person is alone, dependent or cannot say no.
• For each circle, write one safeguard you already have, or one you need.
You will use this map again when you do a risk assessment in Week 5.

ex.t: Example of a circle on a power map
b: Home visit to a child domestic worker: a staff member alone with the child in the employer's house.
Safeguard: visit in pairs, meet in a visible space, debrief afterwards.

units.title: Why Safeguarding Matters: The Nigerian Context and the Human Reasons
units.summary: Learn the legal, practical and human reasons for safeguarding and how to explain them to colleagues in your own words.

sections.h: Why safeguarding matters in Nigeria and Africa
p: Safeguarding is not only a donor rule. It protects real people and strengthens organisations.
• Legal duty: the Child Rights Act, Nigerian labour laws and international standards require it.
• Proof of systems: communities and donors want proof that safeguarding systems are strong.
• Prevention of harm: abuse harms people, so we prevent it. It also prevents loss of life and damage to reputation.
• Saves money and helps raise money: prevention costs far less than a crisis, and strong systems attract funding.
• Protects staff: it protects staff from false accusations and organisations from legal liability.
• Builds culture: a culture of accountability, trust and openness.
• Duty of care: anyone who works with vulnerable groups has this duty, with no exceptions.

b: Which reason matters most to you? Write it on a sticky note or in your notebook.
Why did you choose it? Share your answer with a colleague.

img.alt: A team sitting around a table listening
img.cap: Safeguarding is everyone's job, from leaders to volunteers.

p: When you train others, the human reasons are often more powerful than the legal ones. Use them.
• You are someone's safety net: for a vulnerable person you might be the only one who notices. Your attention could save a life.
• Prevention creates future joy: every child who is protected gets to enjoy childhood and every family kept safe stays whole.
• Safeguarding protects staff too: clear processes protect you from false accusations and from awkward or unsafe situations.
• Cycles of harm stop here: people who are not protected carry pain into adult life. Your action can change a family's story.
• Communities thrive on trust: when safeguarding fails, trust is lost. Your commitment strengthens everyone's sense of safety.
• It is about real people: when you know who you are protecting and why, being alert becomes natural.

ex.t: A short story you can tell
b: A volunteer noticed that a girl in the class stopped speaking and began coming late. He did not ask her directly. He told the safeguarding lead the same day.
The lead spoke to the girl gently, with a second adult, and found she was being harassed on the way home. The family was supported and the problem stopped.
Lesson: small signs matter, and reporting early protects the child.

p: Some people think safeguarding is too expensive or takes too much time. Look at the cost of doing nothing.
• A child is hurt, which is the greatest cost.
• Staff and volunteers may be accused and lose their jobs and good names.
• The organisation may face legal action and lose funding.
• Communities may lose trust and stop sending children to your programmes.
• Other organisations suffer too, because trust in the whole sector is damaged.
The cost of doing it well:
• Time for training, a safeguarding lead with protected time, a small budget for materials and reporting channels.
• These costs are much lower than the costs above.

ex.t: Make the case to your leader
b: Write three sentences: the risk, the cost of doing nothing, the cost of acting.
Use one real example from your own context, without naming people.
Ask for one decision: for example, a named safeguarding lead with time and a budget.

sections.h: What you can do in the next 30 days
p: Start small. These actions cost little and build momentum.
• Read your organisation's safeguarding policy and code of conduct.
• Find out who your safeguarding focal person is, and who the backup is.
• Ask three colleagues if they know how to report a concern.
• Put a reporting poster in one visible place.
• Add a five-minute safeguarding item to your next team meeting.
• Write down one risk in your work and one way to reduce it.
Remember: you do not need to be an expert to begin. You need to care and to act.

b: At the start of every team meeting, ask: 'Is there any safeguarding concern or learning to share?'
Write the answer in the meeting notes.

units.title: International Standards and the Six Core Principles
units.summary: Know the main international agreements that protect children, workers and survivors, and explain the IASC Six Core Principles that most donors expect.

p: International standards are shared promises between countries and organisations about how people must be protected. Nigeria has signed many of them. They give your organisation a strong base for its own policies and show donors you follow accepted practice.
They help you in three ways:
• They tell you the minimum standard you must meet.
• They give you words to use in policies, contracts and training.
• They support you when you say no to harmful local practices.

b: Which of these standards does your organisation already use?
Which ones have you never heard of?

img.alt: A gavel resting on an open law book
img.cap: International standards give a shared base for protection.

p: Learn what each one says in simple words.
• UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC): children's rights to protection from abuse, exploitation and harmful work. Ratified by Nigeria.
• African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child: the African regional standard on child rights and protection. Ratified by Nigeria.
• UN CEDAW: ending discrimination against women, including gender-based violence.
• ILO Conventions 138 and 182: minimum age for work, and the worst forms of child labour, which can include dangerous domestic work. Both ratified by Nigeria.
• ILO Conventions 189 and 190: decent work for domestic workers (189), and freedom from violence and harassment at work (190). Global benchmarks for good practice.
• IASC Six Core Principles and the Core Humanitarian Standard (CHS): the humanitarian standard on sexual exploitation and abuse, and on quality and accountability.
• International Bill of Human Rights: the foundation for dignity, freedom from slavery and servitude, and equal protection.
• 2019 OECD DAC Recommendation: donor commitments on ending sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment in development and humanitarian work.
• IFC Performance Standards: social safeguards for projects covering labour conditions, community health, safety and security.

b: A 12-year-old is working long hours as a house help: ILO Conventions 138 and 182, UNCRC.
A female staff member is harassed at work: ILO Convention 190, CEDAW.
A worker exchanges aid for sex: IASC principles.

sections.h: The IASC Six Core Principles on sexual exploitation and abuse
p: This is the standard that most donors and many organisations expect. Learn all six.
• 1. Sexual exploitation and abuse by aid workers are acts of gross misconduct and are grounds for ending employment.
• 2. Sexual activity with children (anyone under 18) is prohibited, whatever the local age of consent or adulthood. Believing the child was older is not a defence.
• 3. Exchanging money, employment, goods or services (including assistance that people are due) for sex, sexual favours or other humiliating or exploitative behaviour is prohibited.
• 4. Sexual relationships between those providing assistance and the people receiving it are strongly discouraged, because they rest on unequal power and damage trust.
• 5. If a worker has concerns or suspicions about sexual exploitation and abuse by a colleague, they must report it through the proper channels.
• 6. Workers must create and keep an environment that prevents sexual exploitation and abuse. Managers at all levels have special responsibility.

b: A worker says, 'I thought she was 18.' Is this a defence? No, the principle says mistaken belief about age is not a defence.
A worker offers a place on a programme in return for a date. Is this allowed? No, it breaks principle 3.
A worker sees a colleague acting inappropriately but stays silent. What do the principles say? Principle 5 requires reporting.

sections.h: How to use these standards in your work
p: Turn the standards into action.
• Name the standards your policy is based on in the policy itself.
• Use the six core principles in your code of conduct and induction.
• Share them with partners and vendors, and ask them to sign.
• Use them to answer donors and auditors who ask about your standards.
• Review your policy against them every two years.
Remember: the standards are a minimum. Your context may need more.

b: For each activity ask: which standard protects the people involved, and are we meeting it?

units.title: Nigerian and Lagos Law, and the Gap Between Law and Culture
units.summary: Know the main federal and Lagos State laws and structures that protect children and survivors, and understand the barriers that make law hard to apply in practice.

p: Know these laws and what each one means for your work.
• Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999: the right to dignity of the human person (section 34), including freedom from slavery, servitude and forced labour.
• Child Rights Act 2003: the national child protection law. Children may do only light work within the family. It prohibits exploitative labour and abuse.
• Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015: makes rape, physical, emotional and economic abuse and harmful practices crimes, and provides protection orders.
• Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015: makes trafficking and exploitative labour a crime, including children in domestic work. Enforced by NAPTIP.
• Labour Act: limits the employment of children and young persons.
• Cybercrimes Act 2015: makes child sexual abuse material and online exploitation crimes.
• Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023: controls how you collect, store and share personal data, including case and survivor records.

b: A staff member shares a child's photo online with a real name: data protection and Child Rights Act.
An adult offers a 14-year-old a job in another state and takes her away from her family: trafficking law and NAPTIP.
A person is beaten by a spouse: Violence Against Persons Act.

img.alt: Tall stacks of paper files
img.cap: Laws on paper protect people only when they are known and used.

p: Lagos has its own laws and agencies. Learn who does what.
• Child's Rights Law of Lagos State: Lagos domesticated the Child Rights Act. It sets out children's rights, protection duties and the Family Court.
• Protection Against Domestic Violence Law: protects people in domestic settings, which can include children who live and work in a household.
• Criminal Law of Lagos State: sets out sexual offences, including defilement and indecent treatment of children.
• Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency (DSVA): coordinates the response to domestic and sexual violence and supports survivors.
• Ministry of Youth and Social Development: child protection, social welfare and placement of children in need of care.
• Support services: the Office of the Public Defender (free legal help), the Mirabel Centre (sexual assault referral) and the Ministry of Women Affairs and Poverty Alleviation.

b: List the agencies near you, with names and phone numbers, in a one-page referral directory.
Check it every three months. Numbers change.

p: These are not excuses. They are the terrain you work in.
• Law versus culture: child domestic work and child marriage are often accepted socially even where the law limits them. Work with both the law and the reality, without dismissing either.
• Police and justice system: survivors fear reporting because of blame, cost and being hurt again by the process. The system can feel more dangerous than the abuser.
• No regulatory bodies: many sectors have no oversight. Organisations set their own standards, with no outside enforcement.
• Cultural silence and stigma: 'We don't talk about these things.' Shame, family honour and community pressure silence survivors and witnesses.
• Legal gaps and weak enforcement: laws on paper are not protection in practice. Use of the laws differs between states.
• Resources and priority: safeguarding is seen as a donor requirement, and its budget is the first to be cut when funding drops.
Knowing the barriers does not excuse inaction. It helps you plan a smarter approach.

ex.t: A practical response to each barrier
b: Culture: start with the child's welfare and use respectful language.
Justice system: use trusted referral partners and accompany the survivor.
Silence: build safe channels and show that reporters are protected.
Budget: write safeguarding costs into every proposal.

sections.h: Good practice: using the law without being a lawyer
p: You do not need to be a lawyer. You need to know the basics and where to get help.
• Know the age of a child: anyone under 18.
• Know that some acts are crimes, and that you may need to involve police or NAPTIP. Always take the survivor's safety and wishes into account first.
• Keep records safely and share only with people who need to know.
• Keep a list of legal aid and referral services.
• Ask for help: speak to your safeguarding lead and, if needed, a lawyer or legal aid.
• Do not promise outcomes. Say what you can do and what you cannot.

b: I know the age of a child in law.

units.title: Types of Abuse, with Scenarios and Answers
units.summary: Define the five types of abuse and learn to name them correctly in ten real-life scenarios, noticing how power and silence sit at the centre.

p: Learn each type, with its signs.
• Physical abuse: deliberately causing bodily harm or injury, such as hitting, shaking, burning or restraining.
• Emotional abuse: lasting emotional ill-treatment such as humiliation, threats, isolation and constant criticism.
• Sexual abuse: involving someone in sexual activity without consent. It includes exploitation and SEAH.
• Neglect: failure to meet basic needs: food, shelter, medical care, supervision and education.
• Exploitation: using power for personal gain, including labour exploitation and trafficking.
Quick vote: which type is hardest to detect in your work: physical, emotional, neglect or exploitation?

ex.t: Possible signs (they may also have other causes)
b: Physical: unexplained injuries, fear of an adult.
Emotional: withdrawn, low confidence, anxious.
Sexual: changes in behaviour, fear of being alone with a person.
Neglect: hungry, tired, unwashed, missing school.
Exploitation: long working hours, no pay, no freedom to leave.

sections.h: Practise: what kind of abuse is this? (scenarios 1 to 5)
p: Read each scenario. Name the type of abuse (it may be more than one) and be ready to explain why.
• 1. A volunteer at your weekend class for child domestic workers offers one girl 'extra lessons' at his house, alone. (Programme)
• 2. A programme manager refuses to approve travel claims for a staff member who reported his behaviour to the safeguarding lead. (Workplace)
• 3. During community outreach, a field officer tells a 15-year-old house help she will be dropped from the programme if she tells anyone he asked for her number. (Community)
• 4. An aid worker makes food or cash distribution conditional on sexual favours from female caregivers. (Humanitarian)
• 5. A supervisor constantly tells a staff member their work is useless, mocks them in meetings and leaves them out of decisions. (Workplace)

ex.t: Think first, then check the answers below
b: What is the power difference in each case?
What would stop the person from speaking up?
Who might see the warning signs?

sections.h: Practise: what kind of abuse is this? (scenarios 6 to 10)
p: Continue with the next five scenarios.
• 6. A caseworker knows a child domestic worker has not eaten properly for weeks, but does not record it or follow up. (Programme)
• 7. A staff member asks child domestic workers in your programme to wash his car and run his errands, without pay. (Programme)
• 8. A communications officer posts photos of child domestic workers from your programme online, with their real names and the area they live in, without consent. (Programme)
• 9. A community leader who sits on your project committee pressures a girl's family not to report abuse 'for the sake of the family's reputation'. (Community)
• 10. A partner organisation's director repeatedly sends late-night messages with personal comments to junior female staff. (Workplace)

b: 1 Grooming and sexual abuse risk. 2 Retaliation and emotional abuse.
3 Sexual exploitation and abuse of power. 4 Sexual exploitation (SEAH).
5 Emotional and psychological abuse. 6 Neglect (failure to act).
7 Labour exploitation. 8 Digital safeguarding and privacy violation.
9 Emotional abuse and obstruction. 10 Sexual harassment (SEAH).
Notice how often power and silence are at the centre, and how many cases happen inside 'normal' relationships.

p: Look at the patterns.
• Many harms come from people we trust: volunteers, officers, supervisors, community leaders.
• Abuse often begins with small steps such as private contact, special treatment or gifts. This is called grooming.
• Threats of losing support keep people silent.
• Failing to act can itself be harm (neglect).
• Posting images without consent can harm a child long after the event.
• Harassment at work is also a safeguarding issue.
What you should do:
• Name the concern clearly and do not minimise it.
• Report to the safeguarding lead the same day.
• Do not confront the person accused or investigate alone.

b: Can you name the five types of abuse and give one example of each?
Can you spot grooming and retaliation in a scenario?
Do you know who you would tell today?

units.title: Safeguarding Risks for Child Domestic Workers
units.summary: Understand why child domestic workers face special risks, and list the risks in programmes, recruitment, and outreach and online work.

sections.h: Why child domestic workers are at special risk
p: Child domestic workers (CDWs) are children who live and work in other people's homes. They are often hidden, far from their families and dependent on the adults around them.
Key facts:
• They depend on the employer for food, shelter and pay.
• They may not be believed if they speak up.
• Their work may be hidden and not checked by anyone.
• They may be afraid of losing their job or being sent home.
• Anyone who reaches them, including us, holds power over them. That is why our own conduct matters.

b: Reaching a child can itself create risk, for example anger from an employer.
Plan for the child's safety before you make contact.

img.alt: Women sitting together in a meeting room
img.cap: Think carefully with your team about the risks the children you serve could face.

sections.h: Brainstorm: how to find risks with three lenses
p: Work in small groups and list the safeguarding risks that children face when they meet our programmes, people and partners. Use three lenses.
• Lens 1: our programmes and services, including home visits.
• Lens 2: our people and recruitment: who gets access to children, and how.
• Lens 3: our outreach and online work.
For each risk note who is at risk and what type of abuse it is. Then star the three risks that are most serious and most likely.

b: 15 minutes in groups.
5 minutes to share your top three risks.
Keep your list for the risk assessment in Week 5.

sections.h: Risks in our programmes and in recruitment
p: Compare your list with these.
In our programmes:
• Staff or volunteers misuse their access to the child.
• Home visits: staff alone with the child in the employer's house.
• Outreach exposes the child to the employer's anger.
• Consent is asked only from the employer.
• Photos or stories identify the child.
• A child is removed without a safety plan.
In recruitment:
• Unchecked staff, volunteers or drivers reach children.
• No reference or background checks.
• Volunteers are not trained or supervised.
• Hiring is rushed and checks are done late or never.
• Vendors with access never sign the code of conduct.
• Past misconduct is not shared between organisations.

b: Home visits: go in pairs and meet the child in a visible space.
Consent: ask the child and a caregiver in a way that lets them say no.
Recruitment: no unsupervised access until checks are done and training is complete.

sections.h: Risks in outreach and online work
p: More risks to plan for.
• Community volunteers misuse their role with children.
• Outreach exposes a child as a 'case' to neighbours.
• Programme WhatsApp groups are used to reach children privately.
• Staff share personal numbers or follow children online.
• Reporting routes pass only through employers or elders.
• A child is punished at home for joining our activities.
Good practice:
• Use approved platforms and organisation phones.
• No private messaging with children.
• Offer more than one way to report, including a trusted adult outside the employer's household.
• Plan for retaliation and keep contact with the child safe and low profile.

b: Do we always plan for the employer's reaction?
Do we ask the child, not only the employer, for consent?
Do all our volunteers know the rules for contact with children?

units.title: What Safeguarding Needs: Essentials and Safeguarding Assessments
units.summary: See the building blocks of a safeguarding system, the essential first steps, and how to run a safeguarding assessment and turn the gaps into an action plan.
keyWords: In place, partial, not in place

p: A good system has many parts. The starred items below are the core ones every organisation needs first.
Core (starred) parts:
• Safeguarding assessments.
• Safeguarding awareness.
• Policies, procedures and standards.
• Safeguarding culture and leadership.
• Governance and accountability.
• Safe use of media and communications.
• Resources and budgeting.
• Reporting and response mechanisms.
• Safe recruitment.
• Monitoring and consultation.
Other parts to build over time:

• Safeguarding plan, prevention and safe programming, safer spaces, safe partnerships, safeguarding in the supply chain, data protection, ICT and online safety, and continuous learning and improvement.

b: Which of the core parts does your organisation already have?
Which part would make the biggest difference if you improved it this year?

img.alt: Forms and papers on a desk with a pen
img.cap: Assessments, policies and forms turn good intentions into a working system.

p: Start with these.
• Self-assessment tool: assess your safeguarding standing and gaps, then turn the gaps into an action plan.
• Safeguarding budget: put a cost against every planned safeguarding activity so it can be funded, not just wished for.
• Essential policies: write or update the core policies, approved by leadership and signed by staff.
• Assign an SFP/DSL: a named Safeguarding Focal Point (or Designated Safeguarding Lead) with time, authority, support and resources, and a named backup.

b: Month 1: self-assessment and naming the SFP/DSL.
Month 2: draft the action plan and the budget.
Month 3: update the policies and begin induction for all staff.

p: A safeguarding assessment checks how well an organisation carries out safeguarding across policy, culture, practice and systems.
Six areas to check:
• Policy and standards: is there a policy, does it meet the required standards, is it current and easy to find?
• Leadership and culture: do leaders champion safeguarding, and is it safe to speak?
• Training and awareness: are all staff trained, and are communities told of their rights?
• Reporting systems: are there clear, trusted channels with more than one option?
• Response and learning: are concerns answered, followed up, recorded and learned from?
• Safe programming: are risk assessments done and is safeguarding part of programme design?
Status to use for each question: in place, partially in place or not in place.

b: Be honest. An honest list of gaps is more useful than a perfect-looking score.
Ask other people, not only managers, to answer the questions.

sections.h: Live example: assessment and action plan
p: Here is how an anonymous organisation turned gaps into actions in November 2025.

• 1. Does the organisation have a safeguarding policy? Partial. It exists but lacks SEAH provisions and is not aligned with the Child Rights Act. Action: review and revise with SFP/DSL support. Due Dec 2025. Owner: SFP/DSL.
• 2. Has the policy been shared with all staff and volunteers? Not in place. No formal sharing. Action: full induction on the policy, signed copies and tracking. Due Jan 2026. Owner: HR and SFP/DSL.
• 3. Is there a designated Safeguarding Focal Person? In place, but no terms of reference. Action: write terms of reference and set time and reporting line. Due Nov 2025. Owner: Management.
• 4. Are there clear reporting and referral pathways? Partial. Verbal reporting only. Action: written reporting procedure and an anonymous hotline or box. Due Dec 2025. Owner: SFP/DSL.
• 5. Have all staff had safeguarding training in the last 12 months? Not in place. No records. Action: training calendar and mandatory training. Due Feb 2026. Owner: SFP/DSL and HR.
What makes a good action plan:
• Every gap has an action, an owner (a role) and a date.
• It is reviewed every month.

units.title: The Must-Have Policies and What Every Safeguarding Policy Must Contain
units.summary: Learn the eight must-have policies, the seventeen things every policy must contain, and how to run a policy health check.

p: A policy is only as good as its use. These may be one document or several. Together they make up your safeguarding framework.
• Child safeguarding: protects children under 18 in all programmes, activities and interactions.
• PSEAH: prevention of sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment, covering all staff and associates.
• Code of conduct: expected behaviours and clear prohibitions. Everyone must sign.
• Anti-harassment and bullying: deals with bullying, intimidation and discrimination at work.
• Modern slavery: labour exploitation and trafficking risks in programmes and supply chains.
• Whistleblowing: safe, protected ways to raise concerns, with clear protection from retaliation.
• Data protection: how personal and case data is collected, stored, shared and destroyed.
• Reporting procedures: step by step, who does what when a concern is raised.

b: Which of the eight do you have?
Which are one-page statements only, with no steps?
Who approved them, and when?

sections.h: What every safeguarding policy must contain (1 to 5)
p: Use these as a checklist.
• 1. Statement of commitment: a clear statement that safeguarding is a priority, signed by leadership.
• 2. Scope: who is covered, including staff, volunteers, consultants, partners, visitors and all programme settings.
• 3. Definitions of abuse and harm: all five types (physical, emotional, sexual, neglect, exploitation), plus SEAH, unsafe programming concerns and policy breaches.
• 4. Roles and responsibilities: the SFP/DSL, their terms of reference and reporting lines, and what every staff member is personally responsible for.
• 5. Reporting procedure: who reports to whom, by when, through which channel and what happens next. It must include an anonymous option.

ex.t: Example of a good statement of commitment
b: 'We are committed to keeping every child and adult at risk safe from harm caused by our people or our work, and we expect everyone who works with us to share this commitment.'

sections.h: What every safeguarding policy must contain (6 to 10)
p: Continue the checklist.
• 6. Confidentiality provisions: what is kept private, what is shared, with whom and when, including legal exceptions.
• 7. Response and investigation: what happens after a report. Survivor-centred approach, no self-investigation, escalation and timelines.
• 8. Code of conduct: a clear list of expected and prohibited behaviours, signed by everyone covered.
• 9. Safe recruitment provisions: reference checks, disclosure requirements, interview protocols and a safeguarding review in probation.
• 10. Review date and version: reviewed at least every two years, or after any incident. A policy with no review date goes stale.

b: Put the version number and date on every page.
Keep older versions in a folder for audit.

sections.h: What every safeguarding policy must contain (11 to 17)
p: A complete policy also covers how you work every day.
• 11. Safe programming and risk assessment: risk assessments before projects and activities, and who signs them off.
• 12. Partners, vendors and visitors: safeguarding clauses in agreements and contracts, briefings, and rules for visitors and media.
• 13. Communications, media and consent: informed consent for images and stories, and what may never be published.
• 14. Data protection and online safety: how case records and personal data are kept and shared, and safe use of phones and social media.
• 15. Training and awareness: who is trained, when and how often, and how communities and children learn how to report.
• 16. Survivor support and protection from retaliation: medical, psychosocial and legal referral, and protection for anyone who reports in good faith.
• 17. Legal framework: the national, state and donor standards the policy is built on.

b: Take your policy and mark each of the 17 items as in place, partial or missing, with the page number.
Swap with another team for five minutes. Fresh eyes spot gaps.
List your top three gaps, with an owner and a date to fix each.

img.alt: A team around a table with laptops
img.cap: Review your policy together, clause by clause.

o: A fixed fee for every complaint

o: Whenever the organisation changes its logo

units.title: From Policy to Procedure, Tools, Consultation and Practice
units.summary: Turn policy statements into step-by-step procedures, learn the essential tools and templates, and use consultation and monitoring to make safeguarding real.

sections.h: A policy says what; a procedure says who, when and how
p: Policies set the promise. Procedures make it happen.
• Pick one policy statement and break it into the actions it needs.
• Give every action to a role (not a person's name), so nothing is left to chance.
• Set the trigger and timing: 'within 30 days of joining', 'before every activity', 'within 24 hours'.
• Say how: which form, tool, channel or template is used.
• Say where it is recorded and who keeps the record.
• Name who checks, with a review date.
• Communicate and train: share it with the people who must carry it out and build it into induction.

b: Could a new staff member follow it without asking anyone?
If not, add detail.

p: Policy statement: 'All staff and volunteers receive safeguarding training within 30 days of joining.'
Procedure:
• HR or Admin: tells the SFP/DSL about every new staff member or volunteer on the day of joining, by email using the onboarding checklist. Recorded on the checklist. Checked by the line manager.
• SFP/DSL: schedules and delivers the induction training within 30 days, with standard slides and a quiz. Recorded in the attendance register. Checked by management.
• New staff or volunteer: attends the training, reads and signs the policy and code of conduct within 30 days. Recorded in the personnel file. Checked by HR.
• Line manager: confirms there is no unsupervised contact with children until training is done, from day one, using a supervision plan. Recorded in supervision notes. Checked by the SFP/DSL.
• SFP/DSL: reviews the compliance rate every quarter from the training log. Reported to management and the board.

b: Take one clause from your own policy.
Fill in who, does what, when, how, where recorded and who checks.
Share your draft procedure with another team for feedback.

p: A working system uses these every day. Keep them simple.
• Self-assessment tool: your standing and gaps, reviewed each year.
• Safeguarding budget: costs for training, materials, reporting and response.
• Incident report form: records a concern accurately, using what was said and not your opinion.
• Confidential reports register: logs every concern, action and outcome securely.
• Risk assessment template: project and activity risks, owners and reviews.
• Recruitment checklists: reference checks, declarations and induction within 30 days.
• Declaration of acceptance: signed by staff, volunteers and partners after training.
• Attendance registers: evidence of who was trained and when.
• Referral directory: where to refer survivors for health, legal, psychosocial and police help.
• Consent forms: for photos, stories, data and taking part.
• Visibility materials: posters, flyers and child-friendly versions.
• Monthly report template: tracks safeguarding activity, concerns and follow-up.
• Training slides, safeguarding action plan, activity checklist, and the SFP/DSL terms of reference and organisation chart.

b: Pick three tools you do not yet have.
Copy a simple version and adapt it.
Train the people who will use it.

sections.h: Monitoring and consultation: finding out if it works
p: You only know if safeguarding works by asking the people it protects.
• Community consultations: structured talks with adults and children about risks, safe places and how they want to report.
• Surveys and quick polls with participants and staff.
• Focus groups and monitoring visits that include safeguarding questions.
• Feedback boxes and hotlines.
• Monthly safeguarding reports for management.
Findings must go back into your risk assessment and plans, and communities should hear what changed.
Sample questions for consultations:
• How do you feel today? Is anyone uncomfortable taking part? (They can leave without consequences.)
• What does 'being safe' mean to you here?
• What unsafe things could children face during this activity?
• Which places would be safest for our sessions?
• If you saw a staff member or volunteer treat a child in a way that did not feel right, what would you do?
• How would you like to report a concern to us? Would you feel safe doing so?

b: Ask children in ways that suit their age.
Never ask a child to describe abuse in a group.
Always tell them what happened to their suggestions.

p: A policy in a drawer protects no one. Make it live.
• Induction and sign-off: every new person is trained within 30 days and signs the policy and code of conduct.
• Short versions: a one-page summary for staff and a child-friendly version for children and caregivers.
• Visible everywhere: notice boards, offices and community spaces, in local languages, with reporting channels.
• Refreshers: regular briefings, team meeting reminders and yearly refresher training.
• Community sessions: explain your promises and reporting routes to the communities you serve.
• Partners and vendors: share the policy and have it signed as part of every agreement and contract.

b: Is the policy on the notice board in a language people read?
Does every new person sign it in the first month?
Do children know how to report?

units.title: Building and Sustaining a Safeguarding Culture
units.summary: Understand what safeguarding culture is, how to recognise a healthy or unhealthy culture, and five ways to shift culture, including the role of leaders.

p: Safeguarding culture is the shared values, attitudes and everyday behaviours that decide what really happens when no one is checking the policy.
• Why it matters: policies only work where people feel safe to speak up.
• It outlasts people: a strong culture survives staff turnover. A single 'safeguarding person' does not.
• It is a whole system at work: the board oversees, leaders provide resources, the SFP/DSL coordinates, staff follow the code and report, partners comply and communities know their rights.

b: What would a visitor notice about safeguarding in your office or school in the first hour?

img.alt: A large meeting of people around a long table
img.cap: Culture is built when everyone in the system does their part, regularly.

p: Which column sounds more like your organisation?
Signs of a healthy culture:
• People raise concerns early, even small ones.
• Leaders talk about safeguarding without being asked.
• Safeguarding is on routine meeting agendas.
• Reporters are thanked and protected.
• Mistakes lead to learning, not blame.
• Staff can name their SFP/DSL and the reporting channels.
• Communities know how to complain, and do.
• Staff understand their safeguarding role and play it.
Signs of an unhealthy culture:
• 'This doesn't happen here.'
• Safeguarding only comes up after an incident.
• Concerns are handled quietly to protect reputation.
• Reporters are seen as troublemakers.
• Senior staff are treated as above the rules.
• The policy exists, but few have read it.
• Silence is mistaken for safety.

b: Count how many of the 8 healthy signs your organisation has today (0 to 8).
Use signs that are true in practice, not signs written in policy.
Share the totals as a team and choose the weakest sign to improve first.

sections.h: Five ways to shift safeguarding culture
p: Systems do not change culture. People do.
• 1. Leaders must go first: visibly champion it, complete the training, follow the same standards and speak about it openly. Who: board, ED, directors.
• 2. Make it normal, not scary: talk about safeguarding regularly in team meetings, planning and onboarding, not only after incidents. Who: all staff and programme teams.
• 3. Reward speaking up: people who raise concerns feel supported, not isolated or punished. Protection from retaliation is visible. Who: HR, line managers and leaders.
• 4. Build it into every system: recruitment, monitoring, reporting templates, partner agreements, buying and event planning. Who: all functions.
• 5. Give communities a voice: communities know their rights, how to report and trust that reporting is safe. Who: programme and community teams.

ex.t: Which way will you start with?
b: Choose one and write one action for next week.
Example: 'Safeguarding will be the first item at every Monday meeting.'

p: Culture follows what leaders do, not what they sign.
• Champion it: open meetings and induction with safeguarding, and ask about it in every programme review.
• Resource it: budget lines for training, materials, reporting channels, investigations and survivor support.
• Protect the SFP/DSL: give them time, authority, direct access to leaders and the right to escalate.
• Hold everyone to the standard, including senior staff and long-serving colleagues.
• Respond well: acknowledge every report, act on it, and share (safely) what changed because of it.

b: Each organisation shares one thing it already does to keep safeguarding visible.
Choose one small, specific habit to start next week.
Write it on a card and display it.

units.title: Roles and Responsibilities, Job Descriptions and the SFP/DSL Role
units.summary: Know who does what in safeguarding, write safeguarding duties into job descriptions, and understand the full role of the Safeguarding Focal Point or Designated Safeguarding Lead.

sections.h: Everyone has a role, but not the same role
p: Safeguarding is everyone's responsibility, but each group has a different part to play.
• All staff: report concerns, follow the code of conduct, complete training and keep safe behaviour.
• SFP/DSL: receives and records concerns, supports reporters, coordinates the response and keeps records.
• Management: champions culture, makes sure the policy is used, provides resources and holds people to account.
• Board or trustees: oversees governance, carries legal responsibility, reviews safeguarding reports and sets the tone from the top.
• Partners and vendors: sign the code of conduct, attend induction, report concerns and cooperate with investigations.

b: Common functions: board, executive director, SFP/DSL, programmes and case management, MEAL, HR, finance, procurement and drivers, communications and fundraising, grants and partnerships, volunteers and community focal points, admin and security.
Which functions in your organisation are missing from this list?

p: Every function has safeguarding work hidden in its normal job. Write three to five standards for each. Start each with a verb, such as 'Include a safeguarding question in every interview.' Add the evidence an assessor would look for.
What each function is expected to do:
• Leadership: champion culture, approve the policy, resource safeguarding, approve discipline after proven breaches and review safeguarding risks every quarter.

• Human resources: a safeguarding statement in every advert, at least one safeguarding interview question, two reference checks that ask about conduct, signed policy and code of conduct, training within 30 days, refreshers and recorded discipline.
• Programmes and case management: risks assessed for every project and activity, safeguarding in plans, safe locations, child-friendly reporting at every site and community involvement in design.
• MEAL: safeguarding questions in monitoring tools, community consultations, feedback and reporting channels including anonymous ones, and giving answers back to communities.
• Finance: safeguarding budget lines, including survivor support and investigations, and funds that can be reached when needed.
• Procurement, logistics and drivers: safeguarding clauses in vendor contracts, briefings for vendors with access to sites and checks on vehicles and drivers.

• Teachers, community officers, communications, media and fundraising: informed consent for every image and story, never combine a child's full name, location and image, safeguarding sign-off before publishing and briefings for visiting media.
• Grants and partnerships: donor requirements built into design, safeguarding time in every kick-off meeting and partner safeguarding assessed and included in agreements.

b: Culture: ED and board. Continuous improvement: SFP/DSL and management.
Safer programme design: programmes, MEAL and grants. Adequate budget: finance and grants.
Safer recruitment: HR. Safer partners and suppliers: operations and procurement.
Volunteer management: programmes and HR. Risk assessment: programme leads.
Community awareness: programmes. Personal accountability: HR and SFP/DSL.
Reporting and detection: SFP/DSL and MEAL. Case management: SFP/DSL, HR and management.
Survivor support: SFP/DSL.

sections.h: Writing safeguarding into job descriptions and SOPs
p: Make it part of the job, not an extra.
• Start from your function standards and pick the two to four that apply to the role.
• Write them as duties in the job description under a heading 'Safeguarding responsibilities'.
• Add them to the standard operating procedures (SOPs) for that function.
• Set one safeguarding objective in the person's yearly performance plan and discuss it in reviews.
• Update when roles change, so the duty moves with the role, not the person.
Example clause for a Programme Officer:
• Complete a safeguarding risk assessment before every activity involving children or adults at risk, and review it with the line manager.
• Make sure reporting channels are explained at every session and displayed at every site.
• Report any safeguarding concern to the SFP/DSL within 24 hours, and never investigate alone.
• Complete safeguarding refresher training every year.

b: Pick a job in your organisation.
Write three safeguarding duties for it.
Add one measurable objective for the yearly plan.

sections.h: What makes a good SFP/DSL, and what the role covers
p: The Safeguarding Focal Point or Designated Safeguarding Lead coordinates the whole system.
A good SFP/DSL has:
• Skills: knows the policy and law, handles disclosures calmly, keeps accurate records and can train others.
• Authority: can escalate to leaders, pause an unsafe activity and reach the board if needed.
• Access: has time in their workload, a budget line and direct access to leaders.
• A documented role: written terms of reference or job description, a place on the organisation chart and a clear reporting line.
• A named backup, so safeguarding never stops when one person is away.
• The right temperament: trusted, approachable, discreet and willing to raise uncomfortable issues.
Main areas of work:
• Awareness and training: leads induction and refresher training, briefs partners, vendors and visitors, and helps children and communities learn how to report.
• Receiving concerns: first point of contact, records every report in the confidential register within 24 hours.
• Response and referral: makes sure the person is safe first, coordinates the response, refers survivors and escalates.
• Risk and programmes: supports risk assessments and reviews new projects, partners and media content.
• Records and reporting: keeps the register and files safe, prepares the monthly report and reports to donors as agreements require.
• Policy and learning: keeps the policy current, tracks the action plan and shares lessons safely.

ex.t: What the SFP/DSL does and does not do
b: Does: coordinate and advise, make sure the survivor is safe and supported first, keep information confidential, escalate, keep secure records, ask for help.
Does not: investigate alone, carry safeguarding single-handed, act as the survivor's counsellor, decide discipline alone, promise secrecy, ignore a concern because the person is senior.

p: The terms of reference (ToR) and the job description can carry the same content.
• Purpose of the role and who it reports to (ideally the ED).
• Core duties: receive and record concerns, coordinate response and referrals, keep the register, lead training and awareness, support risk assessments and report to management and donors.
• Authority: the right to escalate, pause unsafe activities and reach leaders and the board.
• Time allocation: a set percentage of working time, protected.
• Backup: a named alternate who joins training and can act in their absence.
• Training and support: initial and refresher training, supervision and debriefing.
• Place on the organisation chart, visible to all staff, with contact details shared with communities.

A good model has the board and ED accountable, an SFP/DSL with a deputy, a safeguarding committee, links to HR, legal and wellbeing, and focal points down to schools and communities with confidential reporting channels.
Quick check: can every staff member name the SFP/DSL, the backup and how to reach them? If not, that is your first fix.

units.title: Safe Programming, Risk Triggers and Risk Categories
units.summary: Learn what safe programming means, how it applies across all your work, what a safeguarding risk and a trigger are, and the main risk categories with examples.

p: Safe programming does not mean removing all risk. It means making sure our work does not create or enable harm.
• Safe by design: make every programme, campaign and response safe for the people it reaches.
• No SEAH: programmes must not put children or adults at risk, especially women and girls, of sexual exploitation, abuse or harassment.
• Reduce wider harm: reduce the risk of gender-based violence, trafficking, modern slavery and all abuse within or because of our work.
• Protective environments: strengthen the places where our programmes happen.
• Do No Harm: the most basic principle of ethical programming.
Remember: some risk cannot be avoided. Safe programming is not the same as child protection programming. It cuts across all your work and functions.

b: Design and proposal: think about what the design could create (partners, people, setting, activities) and cost the safeguards.
Start-up: vet staff, volunteers and partners, brief everyone and set up reporting channels before meeting a single child.
Implementation: assess risk before every activity.
Monitoring: ask participants if they feel safe, check the register and update the risk assessment.
Close-out: safe exit for children and families, records stored or destroyed properly and lessons captured.

sections.h: Safe programming across all your work
p: Apply the same thinking to each type of activity.
• Case management: confidential records, safe interviews, informed consent and survivor-centred handling.
• Community outreach: who approves the visit, who goes, how the community knows how to report.
• Home visits: never alone with a child. Visits are planned, logged and supervised.
• Work with child domestic workers: never rely on the employer as the only route to the child. Plan for retaliation.
• Transport: vetted drivers, headcounts, no child alone with a driver, consent for travel.
• Residential activities: separate sleeping by age and gender, supervision rotas and night safety.
• Online engagement: approved platforms only, no private messaging with children and protected data.
• Partners and vendors: safeguarding clauses, briefings and monitoring for anyone with access.

b: Who is at risk?
Who could cause harm?
What could go wrong?
What will we do to stop it, and who is responsible?

img.alt: A team planning around a table with laptops
img.cap: Plan safeguards together before any activity.

sections.h: What is a safeguarding risk, and what triggers it?
p: A safeguarding risk is anything in our work, our people or our environment that could lead to a child or adult being harmed, abused or exploited. A trigger is the situation that sets that risk in motion.
Common triggers:
• One-to-one contact with a child or adult at risk.
• Overnight or residential activities.
• Travel and transport.
• Home visits and outreach.
• Giving out cash, goods or stipends.
• New staff or volunteers brought in quickly.
• Events with photos, filming or media.
• Online platforms and group chats.
• Partners or vendors with direct access.
• Crises such as displacement, price shocks and insecurity.
• Large crowds and unclear supervision.
• Dependence: food, pay or shelter controlled by one person.

b: A risk is the harm that could happen. A trigger is what makes it more likely.
Your plan should deal with the trigger, not only the risk.

sections.h: Risk categories, with one example each
p: Use these categories to make sure you think widely.

• Context and environment: staff or representatives sexually exploit children or adults in the community. Risk factors: norms that accept exchange of money or gifts for sex, high poverty, many children out of school or in domestic work.

• Programme design and implementation: safeguarding is not built into the project, so no capacity or budget exists to prevent or respond. Risk factor: safeguarding left out of the proposal, budget and workplan from the start.
• Partnerships: a partner fails to detect, report or respond to a concern. Risk factors: no reporting system, low commitment from management, no monitoring.
• People: unsuitable people gain access to children. Risk factors: rushed recruitment, no reference checks, volunteers not vetted or supervised.
• Media and communications: a child's identity and location are revealed through a photo or story. Risk factors: no informed consent, name, image and location combined, no sign-off.
• Digital and information: a child is groomed through a programme WhatsApp group or social media. Risk factors: staff unaware of online risks, personal numbers shared, no platform rules.
• Supply chain: an unchecked driver or vendor harms a child. Risk factors: no safeguarding clause in the contract, no briefing, no supervision.

b: Choose one activity.
For each of the seven categories, write one risk that could apply.
Star the two most serious.

units.title: Risk Assessment: Types, Procedure, Scoring and Escalation
units.summary: Learn the four types of risk assessment, follow the six-step procedure, score risks with the impact and likelihood grid, and know when and how to escalate.

sections.h: Four types of safeguarding risk assessment
p: Use the right type at the right time.

• Proposal or programme design: done at design stage. It is not a deep analysis. Think through what risks the design could create from partners, people, setting and activities, and cost the safeguards into the budget. When: before submitting a proposal.
• Organisational: an organisation-wide look at risks across all functions: HR, finance, procurement, communications, programmes and IT. When: yearly, and when things change.
• Project: all the safeguarding risks for one project over its life, with owners and actions, tracked over time. When: at start-up and reviewed every quarter.
• Activity-level: a specific activity or event, such as a school talk, a home visit, a camp or a training. Often a checklist plus a short risk table. When: before every activity.

b: A new proposal to a donor: proposal assessment.
A yearly review of all functions: organisational assessment.
A one-day outreach in a community: activity-level assessment.

sections.h: The risk assessment procedure, step by step
p: Follow six steps.
• 1. Identify the risk. What could go wrong? Ask 'can it happen?', not only 'will it happen?'. Use your categories and triggers.
• 2. Who is at risk? Children, adults at risk, staff, community members. Be specific.
• 3. Rate impact and likelihood, then work out the score and level.
• 4. Plan actions to reduce the risk. Deal with the triggers, not only the risk.
• 5. Name an owner and a date for every action, and the resources needed.
• 6. Review. Before the activity and regularly after. Yesterday's risk is not today's risk.

b: Activity | Identified risk | Who is at risk | Impact | Likelihood | Score and level | Action to reduce the risk | Who is responsible | When due | Resources needed | Last reviewed.

p: Score = (Impact x Likelihood) + Impact. Impact counts twice, so serious harm matters even when it is unlikely.
Impact scale: Negligible (1), Moderate (2), Significant (3), Severe (4), Extreme (5).
Likelihood scale: Rare (1), Unlikely (2), Possible (3), Likely (4), Near certain (5).
Worked examples:
• Severe impact (4) and possible likelihood (3): (4 x 3) + 4 = 16, which is High.
• Extreme impact (5) and rare likelihood (1): (5 x 1) + 5 = 10, which is Medium.
• Significant impact (3) and likely (4): (3 x 4) + 3 = 15, which is High.
• Negligible impact (1) and rare (1): (1 x 1) + 1 = 2, which is Very low.
Risk levels:
• E, Extreme (22 and above): stop or redesign the activity and escalate now.
• H, High (15 to 21): do not proceed without strong action and management approval.
• M, Medium (10 to 14): reduce the risk, assign owners and monitor closely.
• L, Low (5 to 9): manage with routine controls.
• VL, Very low (2 to 4): note and review.

b: Impact 5, likelihood 3: score (5 x 3) + 5 = 20, High.
Impact 4, likelihood 5: score (4 x 5) + 4 = 24, Extreme.
Impact 2, likelihood 3: score (2 x 3) + 2 = 8, Low.

sections.h: A worked example of a risk row
p: Here is one filled row as a model.
• Activity: home visit to a child domestic worker.
• Identified risk: a staff member alone with the child in the employer's house.
• Who is at risk: the child and the staff member.
• Impact: Severe (4). Likelihood: Possible (3). Score and level: 16, High.
• Action to reduce the risk: visits in pairs, meet the child in a visible space, debrief afterwards.
• Who is responsible: programme lead. When due: from the next visit.
• Resources: transport for two staff. Last reviewed: noted with the date.
Good habits:
• Make each row specific to the activity, not generic.
• Make every action realistic, owned and dated.
• Ask others: what risk is missing?

ex.t: Activity: run a full risk assessment on a real activity
b: Choose one real activity, ideally one that reaches children at risk.
Start from your power map and risk list. Add risks for every category and trigger that applies.
Fill in at least five risks with who is at risk, impact, likelihood, action, owner and due date.
Flag anything High or Extreme and write how you would escalate it.
Swap with another team and review: are risks specific, are actions realistic, what is missing?

sections.h: Escalating risk: when, how and to whom
p: Some risks cannot be handled at your level.
When to escalate:
• The risk is High or Extreme.
• You cannot reduce it with the resources you have.
• An incident or near-miss happens.
• The setting changes: a new site, a crisis or a new partner.
How:
• In writing, not just a hallway conversation.
• Update the risk register with the new score.
• Propose a decision: reduce, redesign, pause or stop.
• Record the decision and who made it.
To whom:
• Activity lead to the SFP/DSL.
• SFP/DSL to management or the executive director.
• Executive director to the board for extreme risks.
• To donors where your agreement requires it.
Some risks that are very likely and very serious need you to stop the activity. Pausing to rethink costs less than harm or damage.

ex.t: Ten things to know about risk assessments (1 to 5)
b: 1 Risk assessment is a form of care: think ahead about what could go wrong.
2 Likelihood is not impact: rare events can be fatal.
3 Ask 'can it happen?', not only 'will it happen?'.
4 Some risks mean stopping.
5 Not all risks are obvious: ask participants and stakeholders.

units.title: Safer Spaces, Safe Partnerships and Risk Assessment in Practice
units.summary: Set up safer spaces, build safe partnerships, learn ten practitioner tips for risk assessment, and run risk assessment workshops with your team.

p: A safer space is a place where children and adults can take part without fear.
• Venues are visible and well lit, with safe toilets separated by gender.
• No hidden rooms, and no locked door with a child inside.
• Supervision ratios are set for every activity.
• Visitors sign in, are identified and are never left alone with children.
• Children and staff can be identified (name tags or T-shirts).
• Children are asked where they feel safe and unsafe.

b: Walk around the venue before the activity.
Look for blind spots, unlocked gates, unsafe toilets and unclear exits.
Fix what you can and note what you cannot.

p: Partners and vendors can reach children through your programme. They must meet the same standard.
• Assess a partner's safeguarding before you sign.
• Put safeguarding clauses and your code of conduct in every agreement.
• Include safeguarding time in every kick-off meeting.
• Agree clear reporting lines between you and the partner.
• Monitor, support and review the partner's practice.
• Apply the same expectations to vendors with access to programme sites.

b: Do you have a safeguarding policy and a named lead?
How do you check staff and volunteers?
How do people report concerns to you?
Will you sign our code of conduct?

sections.h: Practitioner's notes: ten things to know (6 to 10 and a recap)
p: Keep these in mind.
• 6. Everyone helps identify risks, not just the safeguarding team.
• 7. Mind the triggers. Your plan should address what sets a risk in motion.
• 8. Incomplete action is an incomplete process. Plans that are not monitored make the assessment meaningless.
• 9. Yesterday's risk is not today's risk. 'We did it last year' is not enough. Update regularly.
• 10. You are probably already assessing risk. You just need to write it down. Documentation is the difference between good intention and compliance.
Recap of 1 to 5: risk assessment is care; likelihood is not impact; ask 'can it happen?'; some risks mean stopping; not all risks are obvious.

b: It is often a skills problem, not a willingness problem.
People skip risk assessments when no one has shown them how.

p: A short workshop builds skill and gets the assessment done at the same time.
• Bring the project team together for one to two hours: programme, MEAL, logistics and community staff.
• Explain the categories and triggers with one worked example.
• Use the risk prompts to brainstorm risks for each category.
• Score and plan actions together, and give owners in the room.
• Agree the review date and put it in the calendar before people leave.

b: A checklist attached to every activity request, signed by a named person and approved by the programme lead.
It covers health and safety, basic needs, activity design, information and accountability and travel.
A short risk table: risk area, rating, controls, likelihood, prevention, owner and deadline.
Completed forms are filed by quarter so they can be checked later.

units.title: Safer Recruitment and Induction
units.summary: Learn why safer recruitment matters and the steps before and after employment: adverts, interviews, references, checks, conditional offers, induction, supervision and exit.

sections.h: What safer recruitment is, and why we do it
p: Safer recruitment is how we block access to people who could harm children or adults at risk, and make sure everyone we bring in is fit to work with children and shares our values. It is one of the strongest forms of prevention we have.
• Block access: people who want to harm children look for organisations with weak checks.
• Fit for children: skills are not enough. Conduct and attitude matter.
• Value fit: people who already believe in dignity and safety are easier to keep safe.
Example safeguarding statement for adverts and job descriptions:

• '[Organisation] is committed to safeguarding children and adults at risk, and expects everyone who works with us to share this commitment. The successful candidate will go through safer recruitment checks, including references and background checks, and must sign our Safeguarding Policy and Code of Conduct.'

b: Why is safer recruitment important? List as many answers as you can in two minutes.

p: Use these steps from advert to offer.
• Advert and job description: a safeguarding statement in every advert, and safeguarding duties in the job description.
• Application form: ask about gaps in employment and why the person left previous roles. Include one safeguarding question.
• Share your policy early: send the policy and code of conduct before the interview so candidates know what you expect.
• Values-based interview: at least one safeguarding question, and a panel member who understands safeguarding.
• Self-declaration: the candidate declares any past allegations, investigations or convictions.
• Reference checks: at least two, including the last employer. Ask directly about conduct with children or adults at risk.
• Background and identity checks: confirm ID and address, check certificates, use guarantors and screen social media.
• Police report and affidavit: a police character report where available and a sworn affidavit of good conduct.
• Role-specific checks: driving test and licence check for drivers, and health checks where the role needs them.
• Misconduct Disclosure Scheme: an inter-agency scheme in which employers share past sexual misconduct findings when asked for references.
• Conditional offer: the offer becomes final only when all checks are back and clear.
• Record it: keep a checks tracker for every hire so it can be audited.

ex.t: A checks tracker (a model, with no names)
b: Columns: staff member | referee check | guarantor check | social media screening | ID and address verification | status.
Each person has a row, with 'completed' or 'cleared' filled in as checks come back.
The tracker is checked by HR and the SFP/DSL.

img.alt: Women sitting around a table in an interview or meeting
img.cap: A good interview panel includes someone who understands safeguarding.

p: Safety continues after the person starts.
• Sign-off: the policy and code of conduct are signed on day one.
• Induction within 30 days, and before unsupervised contact with children.
• Probation with a safeguarding review before confirmation.
• Supervision and appraisal: one safeguarding objective in every plan.
• Refreshers every year, plus briefings when risks change.
• Re-checks when someone moves into a role with more access.
• Exit: exit interviews, and honest references that include proven misconduct.

ex.t: Activity: draft three values-based interview questions
b: Pick a role your organisation often hires for, such as field officer, teacher, driver or volunteer.
Write three questions that begin 'Tell me about a time...' or 'What would you do if...'.
For each, write what a good answer shows and the red flags to listen for.
Example: 'What would you do if a child asked you to keep a secret?' A good answer: listen, explain you cannot promise secrecy and tell the safeguarding lead. A red flag: 'I would keep it between us.'

p: Avoid these.
• Rushing a hire and doing checks later, or never.
• Asking only about skills and ignoring conduct.
• Accepting a reference from a friend of the candidate instead of the last employer.
• Letting a volunteer start work with children before induction.
• Giving a 'good' reference to push out a person with proven misconduct.
• No record of checks, so nothing can be audited.
What to do instead:
• Make safeguarding checks a rule for everyone, including senior staff, volunteers and drivers.
• Keep a checks tracker for each role and review it every quarter.

b: Do all job adverts include the safeguarding statement?
Do we ask for two references and speak to the last employer?
Does anyone work with children before induction?
