units.title: Reporting: Channels People Will Actually Use
units.summary: Learn why reporting matters, why people stay silent, how to fix the barriers, how to set up and share channels that work, and how to read your reporting trends.

sections.h: Why reporting matters, and who reports
p: A concern that is never reported cannot be dealt with.
Why reporting is important:
• It stops harm that is happening now.
• It protects the next child.
• It shows us where our system is weak.
• It builds trust when people see action.
Who reports:
• Staff and volunteers.
• Children and young people.
• Parents and caregivers.
• Communities.
• Partners, vendors and visitors.

b: Draw how a concern travels in your organisation, from the person to the SFP/DSL.
Ask: which channel would a child use? Why that one?
If your funder has its own focal person or hotline, add that line to your map, your posters and partner briefings.

p: Understand the barriers first. There are five groups.
• 1. No feedback culture: no mechanism, no line to report, no one to go to, nothing in place.
• 2. Poor communication: people do not know the channel exists, or how to use it, or that it is for safeguarding. Language is not inclusive and information is not shared well.
• 3. No trust in the mechanism: fear of retaliation or getting in trouble, doubt that reports are received or acted on, doubt that it will be confidential, fair and fast.
• 4. Cultural issues: a false sense of community, not wanting to get another person in trouble, 'we do not do things like that here', silence is normal.
• 5. Context: respect for authority and power distance, fear of stigma, community reputation, money dependence, gender and social norms.

b: A house helper sees a colleague touching a child. She stays silent because the colleague is the madam's relative and she depends on the job. This is a trust, power and money barrier, not a lack of care.

img.alt: Two people having a quiet conversation
img.cap: People report to those they trust. Trust is built before a concern appears.

p: There is no one-size-fits-all fix. Your context matters.

• 1. Assess. Find out what is happening in your organisation. Do people know how to report? Do they feel safe to report? Do they trust the system? Is it inclusive and easy to reach? What are their real worries?
• 2. Identify. Name the real barriers in your context. It may be one, several or something different. Do not guess for people. Let the assessment guide you.

• 3. Act. Remove the barriers and build trust. Strengthen the mechanism, communicate clearly and inclusively, build trust through safety, confidentiality and follow-through, create a real feedback culture, and keep listening to your people.

ex.t: Quick questions to ask in a consultation
b: How would you prefer to report a concern?
Who in this organisation would you trust to tell?
What would stop you from speaking up?

sections.h: How to set up channels that work
p: Follow these six steps.
• Ask first. Run a safeguarding consultation, or add questions to your normal MEAL consultations.
• Create the channels. A dedicated phone line and email, a toll-free or WhatsApp line, an online form, or an internal reporting platform such as KoboToolbox forms.
• Always offer an anonymous option: feedback boxes, anonymous online links or apps.

• Build people-facing routes: community structures, field officers and help desks. For children, a trusted parent or caregiver can be the route. Staff can go to the country lead or any manager they trust.
• Make sure it works, and say how and when: who answers, in what hours, and how fast you will respond.
• Name someone to log every report in the register on the same day.

b: Has someone tested the phone line and the email?
Is the person who answers trained?
Is the box emptied by a named person, on a set day?

p: Every contact is a chance to tell people how to report. Keep something in the community: it speaks when you are not there.
• Posters and notices in offices, schools and community spaces, in local languages.
• Remind people how to report in every session and visit.
• Radio and drama: some organisations use community radio drama to reach families.
• Hotlines and suggestion boxes with an officer assigned to log every report.
• Anonymous channels and a disclosure poster.
• Digital: website, WhatsApp, email signatures and social media.

b: Which is a sign that safeguarding is working: many reports, or no reports?
Answer below.

img.alt: A notebook and pen on a desk
img.cap: Write it down and say it often: people need to hear how to report many times.

p: Read the pattern, not only the number.
• No or very few reports: do not celebrate yet. Troubleshoot. Do people know the channels? Do they trust them? Are the channels working? Ask them.
• Many reports: a healthy sign that people trust the system. Now check the trends: which sites, which activities, which type of concern, which staff?
• Keep a confidential safeguarding incident register. It shows trends over time and tells management where to act.
• Reports often rise after training or new channels. This usually means trust is rising, not that harm is rising.

b: For staff, children, caregivers, community and partners: write which channel each group can use today.
Check: is there an anonymous option? Does every route reach the SFP/DSL, and your funder where needed?
Write three steps to improve reporting, each with an owner and a date.

units.activity: Draw your reporting map for five groups: staff, children, caregivers, community and partners. Mark gaps and write three improvement steps with owners and dates.

check.q: What may a very low number of reports mean?
o: No children are taking part in activities
Staff are fully following the code of conduct
People may not know or trust the channels
Safeguarding is working perfectly everywhere

check.q: Who should log every report in the register?
o: The child who made the report, on paper
A named person, on the same day
Any staff member, within the next month
The partner, at the end of the project

check.q: Why should every system offer an anonymous option?
o: It stops reports from reaching the SFP/DSL
Some people fear retaliation if named
It makes the register shorter for managers
It removes the need to check any report

units.title: Responding to Concerns: Disclosure, Referral and Investigation
units.summary: Know exactly what to do and not do when a child or adult tells you something, how to give a survivor-centred response, where to refer in Lagos, and the basics of an investigation.

sections.h: Receiving a disclosure: dos and don'ts
p: A disclosure is when someone tells you about harm. How you react in that moment matters a great deal.
Do:
• Stay calm, listen and let them speak.
• Believe them and say 'thank you for telling me'.
• Tell them what you will do next and who you will tell.
• Make sure they are safe right now.
• Write down their words, the date and the time, as soon as you can.
• Report to the SFP/DSL the same day.
Do not:
• Promise to keep it a secret.
• Ask leading questions or push for details.
• Investigate, or confront the person accused.
• Show shock, blame or disbelief.
• Share it with anyone who does not need to know.
• Delay.

b: Child: 'Uncle touches me when we are alone.'
Good response: 'Thank you for telling me. I believe you. It is not your fault. I need to tell someone whose job is to keep you safe. I will tell you what happens next.'
Poor response: 'Are you sure? Maybe you misunderstood him.'

img.alt: A child looking out of a window
img.cap: The first reaction a child receives shapes whether they will speak again.

sections.h: A survivor-centred response, step by step
p: Safety, respect, confidentiality and choice at every step.
• Record what was said, in the person's own words.
• Triage: is anyone in immediate danger? Act on safety first.
• Escalate to the SFP/DSL, management and your funder as your procedure requires.
• Refer with consent to health, psychosocial, legal and shelter services.
• Follow up and close the loop with the survivor.
Key ideas:
• Consent: adults decide what happens to them. For children, act in their best interest and involve them as much as is safe.
• Confidentiality: share only what is needed, with those who need it.
• Choice: explain options in simple words and let the survivor choose where they can.

b: Is the person safe now?
Do they need medical care today?
Is the person who harmed them still near them?

sections.h: The Lagos referral pathway for child domestic workers
p: Match the need to the right service. Always check that contacts are still correct in your referral pathway file before use.

• Medical care after sexual assault: sexual assault referral centres in Lagos, such as the Mirabel Centre in Ikeja, the sexual assault referral centre at Alimosho General Hospital, and CeCe Yara Child Advocacy Centre.
• Psychosocial support: the Child Protection Network, Ireti Resource Centre, WARIF, CEWHIN and other community organisations.
• Legal and justice: the Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency, the Lagos State Office of the Public Defender, FIDA Lagos, the Legal Aid Council, the National Human Rights Commission and WARDC.
• Trafficking and emergency rescue: NAPTIP, NACTAL and child protection networks.
• Shelter: child advocacy centres that offer medical care, shelter, rescue and 24-hour support.
• Social welfare and placement: the Ministry of Youth and Social Development and the Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency.
• Education: the State Universal Basic Education Board, the State Ministry of Education and local government education authorities.
• Livelihoods and skills: vocational training and skill acquisition centres.
Memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with these services make referral faster.

b: A girl of 14 reports sexual assault two days ago. List, in order, the three services you will contact first and why.

img.alt: Law books and a gavel on a desk
img.cap: Many cases need legal advice. Know the services before you need them.

p: Keep it simple.
• When is it needed? When someone alleges that a staff member, volunteer or representative has broken the code of conduct or harmed someone.
• Who does it? Trained, independent investigators. Never the SFP/DSL alone, and never anyone connected to the case.
• Timelines: act quickly. Acknowledge, assess and decide within days, not months. Keep the survivor informed.
• Outcomes: fair, tiered sanctions, from warnings and retraining up to dismissal and referral to the authorities.
• Lessons learnt: every case should change something, such as a procedure, a risk assessment or a training.
• Where to get help: Humentum resources, the CHS Alliance PSEAH investigation guidelines and the Safeguarding Resource and Support Hub.

b: You may harm the evidence or put the survivor at risk.
You may be biased or seen as biased.
Untrained interviews can re-traumatise a child.

p: Practise the moment someone tells you something. Rehearsal builds a calm, ready response.
How to run it (20 minutes, groups of three):
• One person discloses using a scenario card, one receives, one observes.
• The receiver responds for 3 minutes, using the dos and don'ts.
• The observer fills in a sheet: what went well and what to change.
• Rotate so everyone plays each role once.

b: Did they stay calm and listen?
Did they avoid promises of secrecy?
Did they explain next steps in simple words?
Did they avoid leading questions?

img.alt: A team listening carefully in a group
img.cap: Good listening is the first skill of a safeguarding responder.

units.activity: With two colleagues, practise the disclosure role-play three times, so each of you plays discloser, receiver and observer. Write down two things you will change.

check.q: Which response to a disclosure is correct?
o: Ask for every detail so you can investigate
Promise to keep it secret between you both
Say thank you and explain what happens next
Confront the person accused in front of others

check.q: Who should carry out an investigation?
o: Trained independent investigators not linked to the case
The manager who supervises the accused person
Any staff member who knows the child well
The SFP/DSL acting alone as the main interviewer

check.q: What should every case lead to?
o: A closed file that no one reads again
A change in procedure, risk plan or training
A public notice naming the people involved
A pause in all activities across all sites

units.title: Resourcing Safeguarding, Fundraising and Safe Use of Media
units.summary: Decide what is safe to post, use the media checklist and the triangle of risk, write safeguarding into proposals, and plan a budget with low-cost and funded items.

p: For each case, decide: post, do not post, or post with changes. Think about why.
• A. A smiling photo of a child domestic worker at a learning class, with her first name and the area she lives in, for a Facebook page.
• B. A donor report case study: 'Aisha, 13, was beaten by her madam in Ikeja', with a photo of her face blurred.
• C. A group photo at a community talk, taken from behind, no names, the place shown only as 'Lagos'.
• D. A video of a crying child telling her story, filmed by a staff member on a personal phone, to raise funds.
• E. A staff selfie with children at an outreach, posted on the staff member's personal Instagram.
Suggested answers:
• A: do not post. First name plus area plus face leads to the child.
• B: do not post as written. A name, age, act and place are still too much, even with a blurred face.
• C: post, with consent and a safeguarding sign-off. No faces, names or exact place.
• D: do not post. A child in distress, a personal phone and a fundraising aim fail dignity and consent.
• E: do not post. Personal accounts and devices are not allowed.

b: Face, name and location.
Never show all three together. Together they lead someone straight to the child.

p: Use this checklist every time.
• Informed consent from the child and the parent or caregiver, in a language they understand. They can say no.
• Dignity: would they be proud of this image in ten years? No distress. No pictures that only show poverty.
• Need to know: does the story need these details at all?
• Pseudonyms and no exact locations. Show the participant the story where you can.
• Use organisation devices and accounts only. Get safeguarding sign-off before anything goes out.
• Data protection: store images securely and delete them when you no longer need them.

b: Poor: 'Tolu, 12, from Makoko, was rescued from a cruel madam.'
Better: 'A girl who used to work in a home now attends a learning class.' (No name, no place, no blame, no face.)

img.alt: Forms and a pen on a desk
img.cap: A signed consent form is only the start. Consent must be informed and can be taken back.

p: Safeguarding must show in the way you ask for money too.
• Proposals: use safeguarding language throughout. Not 'we will employ teachers' but 'we will safely recruit teachers, with references and background checks'.
• Donor visits: brief every visitor on the code of conduct and media rules. Never leave visitors alone with children.
• Case studies: need to know only. Anonymise, use pseudonyms and show the participant their story where you can.

b: Read a sample proposal summary.
Write a safeguarding narrative of no more than 150 words: the risks, how you will prevent them, how people can report, and who leads.
Add at least four budget lines with a short reason for each.

img.alt: A boardroom with people at a long table
img.cap: Donors and boards look for real safeguarding plans inside a proposal.

sections.h: Resourcing safeguarding: not only money, but we still need a budget
p: Low-cost options:
• Experts through your board or pro bono support.
• Build safeguarding into what you already do: meetings, visits, emails, calls and letters.
• MOUs with referral partners and services.
• Shared training with other partners.
What goes into the budget:
• Capacity building, inside and outside, like any other training.
• Community consultations.
• Information, education and visibility materials.
• Reporting channels: phone line, airtime and boxes.
• Survivor support: medical, psychosocial, legal and transport.
• Investigations.
• SFP/DSL time.

b: Line: Reporting channel airtime and box emptying. Reason: so children and caregivers can report free and anonymously.
Line: Annual refresher training for all staff. Reason: skills fade, and risks change.
Line: Survivor transport fund. Reason: so a child can reach a medical centre the same day.

units.activity: Write a safeguarding narrative of no more than 150 words for a project you know, and add four budget lines with one short reason each.

check.q: Which three details must never appear together in public media?
o: Face, name and location
Hobby, village and teacher's name
Gender, language and religion
Age, class and school hours

check.q: Who should be briefed before a donor visit?
o: Only senior visitors from the donor's head office
Only the visitors who plan to meet children
Every visitor, on the code and media rules
Only the staff who drive the visitors around

check.q: Which is a low-cost way to resource safeguarding?
o: Hire an outside firm for every single task
Build it into meetings, visits and routine calls
Delay it until a serious case has occurred
Wait for a new donor to pay for it fully

units.title: Training of Trainers: How Adults Learn and How to Pass It On
units.summary: Understand how adults learn and how behaviour changes, choose from many ways to raise awareness, tailor the message to each audience and plan your first cascade session.

sections.h: How adults learn, and how behaviour changes
p: Adults learn best when the lesson is relevant, practical and builds on what they already know. But information alone rarely changes behaviour. The barrier is often belief, not knowledge.
Eight steps to change behaviour:
• 1. Test the views. Use an anonymous poll or a show of hands first.
• 2. Leave room for questions. Questions are part of learning.
• 3. Validate, then correct. Acknowledge the thought behind a view before you correct it.
• 4. Answer the fear. Speak to what people are afraid of losing.
• 5. Plan for objections. Build the common ones into your session.
• 6. Offer a replacement. Give people something to do instead.
• 7. Rehearse it. Role-play the real moment.
• 8. Follow up. Re-run the questions weeks later.

b: View: 'A child worker needs strict discipline.'
Validate: 'You want the child to grow up well.'
Correct: 'Beating harms children and is against the law.'
Replace: 'Use clear rules, praise and calm talk instead.'

img.alt: A trainer speaking to adults seated in a training room
img.cap: Adults learn by doing, talking and testing ideas, not only by listening.

p: Safeguarding fits into almost any event. Choose the method that suits the audience.
• Induction: every new staff member and volunteer, within 30 days.
• Refresher training: yearly for all staff.
• Briefings: before an activity, for visitors, vendors, drivers and media.
• Project kick-off meetings: safeguarding time at the start of every project and partnership.
• Community awareness sessions: so children, caregivers and communities know their rights and how to report.
• Sector workshops: with schools, employers, transport unions or other groups you work with.
• Team meeting reminders: a five-minute safeguarding item at routine meetings.
• Visibility: website, email signatures, posters, reception screens, online courses and WhatsApp status.

b: New driver: induction and a briefing.
Parents of learners: community awareness session.
Donor visiting next week: a short briefing at arrival.

sections.h: Tailor the message to your audience
p: Whoever you are speaking to, they need four things.
• Who we are: your organisation and what you do.
• What we promise: what is expected of us as an organisation, which is your policy commitment.
• What we expect of you: the participant's role and behaviour, and the information they need.
• How to report: the channels to use when those expectations are not met.
Then adapt the language, length, examples and method. A donor, a driver, a child and a community leader need the same four things, said very differently.
Examples of audiences: children, parents of the children you support, community leaders and elders, employers of child domestic workers, community volunteers, vendors and suppliers, and donors.

b: Children: short sentences, local language or pidgin, pictures, no jargon.
Employers: respectful, direct, focused on the law and the child's rights.
Donors: clear, brief and evidence-based.

img.alt: Sticky notes on a wall used for planning
img.cap: Plan your session on one page: the four things, one story, one question.

p: Teach-back means you deliver a short session to show you can pass the learning on.
How it works (about 45 minutes in total for a group):
• Plan on a one-page template: the four things, one example or story, and one question to check understanding.
• Deliver for five minutes in the language you will use at home. The room plays the audience.
• Peers and the facilitator give feedback: one strength and one suggestion.
• Take home: plan your first cascade session with a date, audience, method, owner and follow-up.
Tips for the trainer:
• Start with a question, not a speech.
• Use a local story, not a foreign one.
• Stop to check: 'What would you do?'
• End with the one thing you want people to remember and how to report.

b: Audience | Date | Method | Language | Who leads | Materials needed | Follow-up date.

units.activity: Write a five-minute awareness session for one audience in your organisation using the four things. Deliver it to a colleague and ask for one strength and one suggestion.

check.q: What often blocks behaviour change?
o: A shortage of printed posters in offices
Belief, not only a lack of knowledge
The length of the training session slides
The number of people in the training room

check.q: Which is one of the four things every audience needs?
o: The history of the funding donor
The list of past complaints received
How to report a concern
The salary scale of all staff

check.q: What is the purpose of a follow-up with learners?
o: Collect the printed notes from everyone
Close the session file for the year
Repeat the same slides word for word
Re-test views and see what has changed

units.title: Owning It: Your 90-Day Action Plan and Closing the Course
units.summary: Turn learning into action with owners and dates, track your plan, plan for succession, and prepare for the end-of-course assessment.

p: A plan on paper does not protect anyone. A plan that is owned and tracked does.
• Owners, not intentions. Every action has a named role and a date.
• Track it. Use a simple tracker reviewed monthly, alongside your safeguarding report.
• Check in with management. Make safeguarding a standing item at management meetings.
• Plan for succession. Name a backup for the SFP/DSL and keep handover notes, so progress survives staff changes.

b: What has helped you stay on top of action plans before?

img.alt: A team planning at a table
img.cap: Plans are kept alive in regular team meetings, not in drawers.

p: Choose a few actions you can really finish in 90 days.
• Days 1 to 30: brief your management, share what you learned, and fix one quick win such as a poster with reporting channels.
• Days 31 to 60: run your first risk assessment workshop and start your safeguarding register.
• Days 61 to 90: deliver your first cascade session and review progress with management.
For each commitment write: what, who, by when, what help is needed and how you will know it is done.
Examples:
• Add a safeguarding statement to every job advert by day 30.
• Complete an activity risk assessment for the next home visit.
• Hold one staff awareness session using the four things.
• Name and train a backup for the SFP/DSL.

b: Action | Owner | Due date | Help needed | Done when | Status.

p: The final assessment has 100 questions. It tests understanding and judgement, not memory alone.
How to prepare:
• Review the key words at the top of each unit.
• Re-do your activities and the unit practice questions.
• Practise the scoring formula and the risk levels.
• Review the dos and don'ts for disclosure and the checklist for media.
• Read each question and all four options slowly. Several options may look right. Choose the one that fits best.
About the questions:
• Options are written to look alike in length, so you cannot guess from the length of an answer.
• Many questions use short real-life situations.
• You need 75 percent to pass.

b: Safeguarding is everyone's job, and every report matters.
Believe, listen, report the same day, and keep confidentiality.
Never promise secrecy and never investigate alone.
Be the person a child can safely tell.

img.alt: Files and documents stacked in a cabinet
img.cap: Keep your notes, templates and plans together for easy review.

units.activity: Fill in your 90-day action tracker with at least five actions, each with an owner and a date. Name a backup for the SFP/DSL and set the date of your first management check-in.

check.q: What makes an action in a plan reliable?
o: A strong wish to complete it soon
A named owner and a due date
A mention in the annual newsletter
A long description in the report

check.q: Why should the SFP/DSL have a named backup?
o: So reports can be delayed for weeks
So the SFP/DSL can avoid all meetings
So donors can contact two people
So progress survives staff changes

check.q: How often should the action tracker be reviewed?
o: Every five years with the policy
Once, at the end of the project
Monthly, with the safeguarding report
Only after a serious incident occurs

questions.q: A volunteer offers one girl private lessons alone at his house. How should this be classed?
o: A security issue because the lessons happen without supervision
An HR matter because volunteers must follow staff schedules
A safeguarding concern because our own volunteer creates risk
A safety issue because the house may lack exits
questions.why: Safeguarding covers harm risked by our own people and activities.

questions.q: Which difference separates safeguarding from child protection?
o: Safeguarding replaces all police work whenever children face harm
Safeguarding covers only harm happening inside private family homes
Safeguarding reacts only after harm to one named child
Safeguarding acts before harm for all children at risk
questions.why: Safeguarding is broader and acts before harm, covering harm caused by us or our work.

questions.q: Staff sign the code, risk assessments precede activities and drivers are vetted. Which pillar is mainly shown?
o: Awareness, because people learn what harm looks like there
Prevention, because harm is stopped before it can happen
Response, because survivors receive quick and correct action here
Reporting, because concerns are raised through safe channels now
questions.why: Risk assessments, codes and vetting are prevention measures.

questions.q: Which action belongs to the Response pillar?
o: Training new volunteers in induction before they meet any children
Posting reporting channels on every notice board in local languages
Completing activity risk assessments before every single home visit begins
Following the policy, escalating the case and never investigating alone
questions.why: Response means acting correctly: follow policy, escalate, and do not investigate alone.

questions.q: A field officer promises registration on a list in return for time with a mother. Which term fits best?
o: Sexual exploitation, because he abuses unequal power for gain
Social safeguard, because he registered families under project rules
Sexual harassment, because the behaviour occurs between two colleagues
Neglect, because he failed to meet her basic needs
questions.why: Exploitation is abuse of unequal power or trust for gain.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
o: A teacher hitting pupils; a general safety issue only
A late vendor payment; a safeguarding concern for children
A broken fire exit; a child protection case today
A stolen laptop; a security issue for the organisation
questions.why: Theft is security. A teacher hitting pupils is a safeguarding issue.

questions.q: What does 'Do No Harm' require of an organisation?
o: Staff must always answer to donors before affected communities
Presence and programmes must never make people less safe
Managers must act only when harm is formally proven
Projects must avoid all risk of any kind whatsoever
questions.why: Do No Harm means our work must never leave people less safe.

questions.q: Which statement about accountability is correct?
o: Staff report upward but communities are never told anything
Complaints are recorded but no one needs to respond
Communities know what to expect and can give feedback
Donors alone decide whether a community complaint was valid
questions.why: Accountability means being answerable to the people we serve, not only to donors.

questions.q: A supervisor asks a junior colleague for a favour while holding her contract renewal. Why is her yes doubtful?
o: Fear of losing the contract can remove her free choice
Contract renewals always require written consent from both senior colleagues
Junior staff cannot give consent to any request at work
Supervisors automatically lose their authority when they ask for favours
questions.why: Consent is only real when a person is free to say no.

questions.q: Which statement about power is most accurate?
o: Power comes from money alone, so age and gender never really matter
Power shifts with context, so one person can hold little or much
Power belongs only to managers, so volunteers and drivers never hold any
Power is fixed by job title, so context never really changes it
questions.why: Power has many sources and changes with the setting.

questions.q: A driver is alone with a child travelling to an activity. Which safeguard is most direct?
o: Faster routes, tinted windows and quiet music during trips
Cheaper vendors, longer contracts and no briefings for drivers
Vetted drivers, headcounts and no child alone with drivers
Private phones, personal numbers and direct messages with children
questions.why: Vetting, headcounts and never leaving a child alone with a driver reduce the risk.

questions.q: A mother is told her name goes on the list if she spends time with the officer. What is true?
o: Her agreement is not free consent because he controls support
Her agreement is valid consent because she is an adult
Her agreement is valid consent because the offer was optional
Her agreement is valid consent because she said it aloud
questions.why: Control of support removes free choice, so her yes is not consent.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a power map?
o: It ranks staff by seniority so managers can set pay bands
It shows where harm could happen and safeguards must be strongest
It lists donors by funding size so reports can be sorted
It maps office floors so fire exits are easy to find
questions.why: A power map shows who holds power over whom, so safeguards go where risk is highest.

questions.q: Which question is most useful when examining a relationship for power?
o: Who owns the vehicle and pays the monthly running fuel costs?
Who can leave and who would be believed if harm happened?
Who speaks the loudest and attends the most weekly staff meetings?
Who earns the highest salary and holds the longest running contract?
questions.why: Leaving and being believed are the key tests of power in a relationship.

questions.q: Which argument best persuades a leader who says safeguarding costs too much?
o: Staff will accept lower pay when safeguarding rules are very strict
Donors will only fund organisations that publish every single incident openly
Prevention costs far less than lost trust, funding and legal liability
Governments will immediately close organisations that lack a printed policy document
questions.why: The cost of doing nothing is far higher than the cost of prevention.

questions.q: Which cost of doing nothing is the greatest?
o: A child is hurt, which no budget can repair
A policy expires, which no committee can quickly repair
A brand loses value, which no campaign can repair
A donor cuts funding, which no report can repair
questions.why: Harm to a child is the greatest cost.

questions.q: A 12-year-old works long hours as a house help. Which standards apply most directly?
o: ILO Convention 190 and CEDAW provisions on workplace harassment
ILO Conventions 138 and 182, plus the UNCRC protections
IASC principles and the Core Humanitarian Standard on exploitation
IFC Performance Standards and the 2019 OECD donor recommendations
questions.why: Minimum age and worst forms of child labour are covered by ILO 138 and 182 and the UNCRC.

questions.q: A worker says 'I thought she was 18.' What do the IASC principles say?
o: Honest belief reduces the sanction but not the breach
Written proof of age from the girl is enough
Mistaken belief about age is never a valid defence
Local custom on adulthood decides whether a defence applies
questions.why: Principle two says a mistaken belief about age is not a defence.

questions.q: Which IASC principle requires reporting of a colleague's suspected misconduct?
o: Principle six, which holds managers responsible for environment
Principle three, which bans exchanging aid for favours
Principle four, which discourages relationships with aid recipients
Principle five, which requires reporting through proper channels
questions.why: Principle five requires workers to report concerns through proper channels.

questions.q: An aid worker offers a programme place in return for a date. Which principle does this most directly break?
o: Principle two, because it involves a child under eighteen
Principle three, because it exchanges assistance for sexual favours
Principle four, because a relationship with the recipient formed
Principle five, because the worker failed to report staff
questions.why: Principle three bans exchanging assistance for sex or favours.

questions.q: How should an organisation use international standards?
o: Name them in donor reports and update the policy when audited
Replace local policies with them and drop all local rules entirely
Treat them as the maximum and never exceed their stated limits
Name them in policy and review the policy every two years
questions.why: Standards are a minimum that should be named in the policy and reviewed.

questions.q: Which standard sets out freedom from violence and harassment at work?
o: ILO Convention 190, which covers violence and harassment at work
ILO Convention 138, which covers the minimum age for work
ILO Convention 189, which covers decent work for domestic workers
ILO Convention 182, which covers worst forms of child labour
questions.why: ILO 190 deals with violence and harassment at work.

questions.q: A 14-year-old is offered a job in another state and taken from her family. Which law and agency apply?
o: Cybercrimes Act, enforced by national data regulators
Labour Act, enforced by local employer associations
Violence Against Persons Act, enforced by police
Trafficking in Persons Act, enforced by NAPTIP
questions.why: Trafficking is covered by the Trafficking in Persons Act and enforced by NAPTIP.

questions.q: A staff member shares a child's photo online with a real name. Which laws are most relevant?
o: The Labour Act and the Violence Against Persons Act
Data Protection Act 2023 and the Child Rights Act
Only the Lagos Criminal Law on sexual defilement offences
The Trafficking Act and the Constitution's free movement provisions
questions.why: Sharing identifiable images breaks data protection and child rights law.

questions.q: Which agency coordinates the Lagos response to domestic and sexual violence?
o: The Family Court, which investigates every reported abuse case
The Public Defender's office, which licenses private safe houses
The Mirabel Centre, which prosecutes every sexual offence case
The Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency, which supports survivors
questions.why: The DSVA coordinates the response and supports survivors.

questions.q: Why is the gap between law and culture a challenge?
o: Practices like child domestic work stay accepted despite legal limits
Communities already follow every law so outreach is largely unnecessary
Laws are unenforceable and should therefore be ignored in practice
Culture is always harmful and must be rejected by staff
questions.why: Social acceptance can continue even where the law limits a practice.

questions.q: A survivor fears the police process. What is the best practical response?
o: Report to police immediately without asking what she wants
Close the file because she declined to proceed formally
Promise her that the case will certainly end successfully
Use trusted referral partners and accompany the survivor throughout
questions.why: Accompany the survivor, use trusted partners and respect her wishes. Never promise outcomes.

questions.q: Which approach to using the law without being a lawyer is correct?
o: Avoid the police completely because cases are always mishandled in Lagos
Promise outcomes early so that survivors can feel confident and calm
Know the child's legal age and keep a legal referral list
Share every record widely so lawyers can see the full picture
questions.why: Know the basics, keep a referral list and never promise outcomes.

questions.q: A caseworker knows a child has not eaten properly for weeks but records nothing. Which type of harm is this?
o: Exploitation, because the caseworker clearly gained money from her hunger
Emotional abuse, because silence always damages the child's growing confidence
Physical abuse, because hunger deliberately causes bodily injury to her
Neglect, because failing to act on basic needs is harm
questions.why: Failing to meet or act on basic needs is neglect.

questions.q: A manager refuses the travel claims of a staff member who reported his behaviour. How is this best described?
o: A routine finance decision, which is clearly outside safeguarding scope
Retaliation against a reporter, which is itself abuse of power
A legitimate budget control, which applies equally to all staff
A performance matter, which should wait for the annual review
questions.why: Punishing a reporter is retaliation and a misuse of power.

questions.q: Which pattern best describes grooming?
o: Regular supervised lessons run by two trained adult volunteers
Small steps like private contact, gifts and special treatment
Open praise given equally to every child at events
A single violent act committed in public by strangers
questions.why: Grooming starts with small steps such as private contact, gifts and special treatment.

questions.q: A communications officer posts photos of child domestic workers with real names and areas, with no consent. Which label fits best?
o: Minor policy slip because no physical harm occurred yet
Acceptable promotion because the photos clearly support fundraising goals
Digital safeguarding failure and a privacy violation of children
Labour exploitation because the children received no direct payment
questions.why: Posting identifiable images without consent is a digital safeguarding and privacy failure.

questions.q: A community leader pressures a family not to report abuse for reputation. What is this?
o: A cultural duty that organisations must not question
Obstruction of reporting that can add emotional harm
A private matter outside safeguarding and community concern
A respected mediation that protects family honour fairly
questions.why: Blocking a report protects the abuser and adds harm.

questions.q: You notice signs of abuse by a trusted volunteer. What should you do?
o: Confront the volunteer privately and demand an explanation
Report to the safeguarding lead the same day
Wait for more evidence before telling anyone senior
Investigate quietly and interview the child about details
questions.why: Report the same day and never confront or investigate alone.

questions.q: Which set of signs is most associated with exploitation of a child worker?
o: Unexplained injuries, a fear of one adult and sudden withdrawal
Withdrawn behaviour, low confidence and visible anxiety around other adults
Long working hours, no pay and no freedom to leave
Missing school, looking tired, unwashed and arriving hungry each day
questions.why: Exploitation shows as long hours, no pay and no freedom to leave.

questions.q: Which scenario is sexual exploitation under SEAH?
o: Cash distribution made conditional on sexual favours from caregivers
A staff member asking children to wash his car
A supervisor mocking a staff member in team meetings
A communications officer posting photographs without any parental consent
questions.why: Making aid depend on sexual favours is sexual exploitation.

questions.q: Why are child domestic workers at special risk?
o: They usually choose their work with full family support
They depend on employers for food, shelter and pay
They are well known to police and social workers
They live in organised groups with regular adult supervision
questions.why: Dependence on the employer, being hidden and not being believed raise their risk.

questions.q: Before contacting a child domestic worker, what must the team plan for?
o: The donor report, including the number of children reached
The press release, including the programme's expected media coverage
The child's safety, including the employer's likely angry reaction
The staff schedule, including the times of employer meetings
questions.why: Reaching the child can create risk, so plan for her safety first.

questions.q: Which reporting design is safest for child domestic workers?
o: One route passing through village elders for cultural fit
One route using only the staff member's personal phone
Several routes including a trusted adult outside the household
One route passing through the employer for quick approval
questions.why: Offer more than one route, including a trusted adult outside the employer's home.

questions.q: Which is the correct consent practice for child domestic workers?
o: Ask the child once and treat the answer as permanent forever
Ask the child and a caregiver in a way allowing refusal
Ask only the employer because the employer legally controls the child
Ask staff members who know the family well to decide instead
questions.why: Ask the child, not only the employer, in a way that lets them say no.

questions.q: Which set lists the four essential first steps for an organisation?
o: Board dinner, website design, fee increase and a named bank
A self-assessment, a budget, essential policies and a named SFP/DSL
Donor visit, press launch, staff party and a named mascot
Annual report, new logo, office lease and a named auditor
questions.why: Start with a self-assessment, a budget, essential policies and a named SFP/DSL.

questions.q: A policy exists but has no steps, no SEAH provisions and is not shared. How should this be rated?
o: Not applicable, because policies need not always include SEAH
In place, because a policy document has been written
In place, because staff can request it if needed
Partial, because it exists but important parts are missing
questions.why: A policy that exists but lacks key content and sharing is only partially in place.

questions.q: What makes a safeguarding action plan reliable?
o: Every gap has a meeting, a chairperson and a minute book
Every gap has an action, an owner role and a date
Every gap has a wish, an owner name and a hope
Every gap has a report, a donor and a fixed deadline
questions.why: Actions need an owner (a role) and a date, and monthly review.

questions.q: Who should answer self-assessment questions for the most honest picture?
o: Only senior managers, answering for all staff
Only the SFP/DSL, answering from memory alone
Only the board, answering from past reports
Many people, not only managers, answering honestly
questions.why: Ask other people, not only managers, and be honest about gaps.

questions.q: Which policy deals with safe ways to raise concerns, with protection from retaliation?
o: Modern slavery, with steps on supply chain risks
Anti-harassment, with clear rules on workplace bullying behaviour
Whistleblowing, with clear protection from retaliation for reporters
Data protection, with rules on storing case records
questions.why: The whistleblowing policy protects people who raise concerns in good faith.

questions.q: When should a safeguarding policy be reviewed?
o: Never, because a signed policy stays valid for ever
Every ten years alongside the long strategic plan cycle
Only when a donor requests a fresh signed version
At least every two years or after any incident
questions.why: Policies should be reviewed at least every two years or after an incident.

questions.q: What should the scope of a safeguarding policy cover?
o: Permanent staff only, in the head office and sites
Staff, volunteers, consultants, partners, visitors and every programme setting
Children only, in classroom settings run by the organisation
Staff and volunteers only, during working hours at sites
questions.why: The scope must include everyone linked to the organisation, in every setting.

questions.q: What should confidentiality provisions in a policy state?
o: That information is shared only when a donor requests a copy
That all details are shared with every staff member for transparency
That nothing is ever shared with anyone, including the police authorities
What is private, what is shared, with whom, including legal exceptions
questions.why: Confidentiality means sharing only what is needed with those who need it, with legal exceptions.

questions.q: Who should sign the statement of commitment in a policy, and why?
o: The donor's representative, showing that funders approve every policy
The SFP/DSL alone, showing that safeguarding is specialist work
Leadership, showing that safeguarding is a clear organisational priority
The newest staff member, showing that everyone shares responsibility
questions.why: Leadership signs to show safeguarding is a priority.

questions.q: Which feature must a reporting procedure include?
o: A verbal route only, with no written records kept
A donor route only, with no internal staff channel
A single named channel, with strict office hours only
An anonymous option, plus who reports to whom, when
questions.why: A reporting procedure needs clear steps, timelines and an anonymous option.

questions.q: A policy says staff are trained within 30 days. What does a procedure add?
o: A longer promise, a bolder tone and a signed leadership letter
Who acts, when, how, where it is recorded and who checks
A legal opinion, a court filing and a sworn notarised copy
A donor logo, a printed cover and a numbered page layout
questions.why: A procedure adds who, when, how, where recorded and who checks.

questions.q: In the 30-day training example, who confirms there is no unsupervised contact until training is done?
o: The donor, using a monitoring checklist from the first month
The new volunteer, using a self-declaration form on day one
The board, using an annual audit from the first year
The line manager, using a supervision plan from day one
questions.why: The line manager confirms this using a supervision plan from day one.

questions.q: Which consultation practice is correct with children?
o: Ask only caregivers and then summarise the children's views on their behalf
Ask in age-suitable ways and never ask for abuse details in groups
Ask in group sessions and require each child to describe any harm
Ask once a year and then never report back on what changed
questions.why: Ask children in age-suitable ways and never ask them to describe abuse in a group.

questions.q: What should happen to findings from safeguarding consultations?
o: Be used only to design the next donor fundraising campaign
Feed into risk assessments and plans, with feedback to communities
Be summarised for the board but hidden from the communities
Stay in the report folder until the next donor visit
questions.why: Findings must go back into risk assessments and plans, and communities should hear what changed.

questions.q: Which is a sign of an unhealthy safeguarding culture?
o: Safeguarding sits on routine meeting agendas every month
Reporters are thanked, protected and told what changed
Concerns are handled quietly to protect organisational reputation
Mistakes lead to open learning rather than blame
questions.why: Handling concerns quietly to protect reputation is a sign of an unhealthy culture.

questions.q: Which is the first of the five ways to shift safeguarding culture?
o: Donors go first by writing much stricter conditions into contracts
Communities go first by reporting before any training ever happens
Leaders go first by visibly championing and following the standards
Staff go first by reporting every colleague's small mistake publicly
questions.why: Leaders must go first and follow the same standards.

questions.q: A senior staff member breaks the code and a leader says he has served for years. What does a healthy culture require?
o: Delay action until the donor has finished its current review
Hold everyone to the same standard, including long-serving senior staff
Allow a quiet warning because seniority earns some extra tolerance
Move him to another site so the problem leaves quietly
questions.why: Leaders must hold everyone to the standard, including senior staff.

questions.q: Why does a strong culture outlast individual people?
o: Shared values survive staff turnover, but one lead does not
Donor funding survives staff turnover, but local trust does not
Signed forms survive staff turnover, but daily habits do not
Written policies survive staff turnover, but shared values do not
questions.why: A single safeguarding person leaves, but shared values and habits remain.

questions.q: Which duty belongs to the board or trustees?
o: Deliver all induction training and brief every visiting vendor
Receive every concern first and record it in registers
Oversee governance, carry legal responsibility and review safeguarding reports
Collect reference checks and keep every personnel file safe
questions.why: The board oversees governance, carries legal responsibility and reviews reports.

questions.q: Which action is NOT part of the SFP/DSL role?
o: Escalate concerns to leaders and refer survivors to support services
Investigate serious allegations alone to save the organisation precious time
Lead induction training and brief partners, vendors and visiting guests
Record each report in the confidential register the same day
questions.why: The SFP/DSL never investigates alone.

questions.q: What gives an SFP/DSL real authority?
o: Right to escalate, pause unsafe activities and reach the board
A title on the door and a mention in handbooks
A donor letter and a place on the finance committee
Personal friendship with the director and a flexible office timetable
questions.why: Authority means the right to escalate, pause unsafe activities and reach the board.

questions.q: Which job description clause is best for a Programme Officer?
o: Be aware of safeguarding issues and try to avoid any very serious mistakes
Attend safeguarding training when invited and share the slides with your close colleagues
Complete a risk assessment before every activity involving children or adults at risk
Support the safeguarding team whenever time allows during the normal busy working week
questions.why: A good clause is specific, measurable and tied to the work.

questions.q: What should the yearly performance plan include?
o: No safeguarding objective because it belongs in the policy
One safeguarding objective for each person, discussed in reviews
One safeguarding objective for the SFP/DSL, discussed once yearly
A safeguarding objective only for staff meeting young children
questions.why: Every yearly plan should carry one safeguarding objective, reviewed with the line manager.

questions.q: Which set describes a well-formed SFP/DSL role?
o: A part-time post, fixed duties and no budget line allowed
A named backup, protected time and direct access to leaders
A volunteer deputy, flexible time and indirect access to leaders
A single holder, unlimited duties and full authority over discipline
questions.why: A good role has a backup, protected time and direct access to leaders.

questions.q: What does safe programming aim to do?
o: Limiting all contact between staff and children at distant sites
Removing every risk so that no activity can ever fail
Replacing child protection programmes with general site safety measures only
Making sure our work does not create or enable harm
questions.why: Safe programming does not remove all risk. It ensures our work does not create or enable harm.

questions.q: A school plans an overnight camp. What is the trigger for a safeguarding risk?
o: The harm a child could suffer during the night
The camp fee that families must pay before travel
The overnight stay, which creates unsupervised contact at night
The reputation damage that follows after a serious incident
questions.why: A trigger is the situation that sets a risk in motion.

questions.q: Staff share personal numbers and a group chat allows private contact with children. Which risk category fits?
o: Context and environment, because the community accepts online chatting
Partnerships, because partners always manage the group chat settings
Supply chain, because vendors supply the phones used there
Digital and information, because online channels allow private contact
questions.why: Online platforms and personal numbers are digital and information risks.

questions.q: Rushed recruitment, no reference checks and unsupervised volunteers belong to which category?
o: People, because unsuitable individuals gain access to children
Programme design, because safeguarding is missing from budget
Supply chain, because vendors have no safeguarding clause
Media, because a child's identity may be revealed
questions.why: Weak recruitment lets unsuitable people reach children, which is a people risk.

questions.q: At which stage do teams ask participants if they feel safe and check the register?
o: Start-up, which also vets staff and partners
Design, which also costs the mitigation properly
Close-out, which also stores all records safely
Monitoring, which also updates the risk assessment
questions.why: Monitoring checks safety, the register and trends, and updates the risk assessment.

questions.q: Which rule is correct for home visits to child domestic workers?
o: Visits are skipped whenever the employer objects to access
Visits are planned, logged, supervised and never made alone
Visits are spontaneous, informal, private and usually made alone
Visits are arranged through employers who stay in rooms
questions.why: Home visits must be planned, logged and supervised, and never made alone.

questions.q: A risk has Severe impact (4) and Likely likelihood (4). What are the score and the response?
o: 24, rated Extreme, needing immediate stop and escalation
16, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
20, rated Extreme, needing immediate stop and escalation
20, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
questions.why: (4 x 4) + 4 = 20, which is High (15 to 21).

questions.q: A risk has Extreme impact (5) but Rare likelihood (1). What is the result?
o: 15, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
6, rated Low, needing only routine controls here
10, rated Medium, needing mitigation, owners and monitoring
5, rated Low, treated like merely negligible impact
questions.why: (5 x 1) + 5 = 10, which is Medium. Impact counts twice.

questions.q: A risk has Significant impact (3) and Likely likelihood (4). What is the result?
o: 12, rated Medium, needing mitigation, owners and monitoring
9, rated Low, needing only routine controls here
18, rated High, needing immediate stop and escalation
15, rated High, needing strong mitigation and sign-off
questions.why: (3 x 4) + 3 = 15, which is High.

questions.q: A risk has Moderate impact (2) and Possible likelihood (3). What is the result?
o: 12, which is Medium and needs owners and monitoring
8, which is Low and managed with routine controls
6, which is Low and managed with routine controls
10, which is Medium and needs owners and monitoring
questions.why: (2 x 3) + 2 = 8, which is Low (5 to 9).

questions.q: Which formula gives the safeguarding risk score?
o: Impact multiplied by likelihood, then impact added again
Impact multiplied by likelihood, then divided by impact
Likelihood multiplied by impact, then likelihood added again
Impact added to likelihood, then the total doubled
questions.why: Score = (Impact x Likelihood) + Impact.

questions.q: Why does the formula add impact a second time?
o: Unlikely events should always be ignored by planning teams
Frequent small harms should always outweigh rare severe harms
Serious harm should still matter when it is unlikely
Donors prefer scores that reach higher numbers on charts
questions.why: Impact counts twice so that serious harm still matters when it is unlikely.

questions.q: Which score range means the activity must be stopped or redesigned and escalated now?
o: 10 to 14, rated Medium on the grid
22 or above, rated Extreme on the grid
5 to 9, rated Low on the grid
15 to 21, rated High on the grid
questions.why: Extreme (22 and above) needs a stop or redesign and immediate escalation.

questions.q: Which risk has the highest score?
o: Significant impact paired with near certain likelihood
Extreme impact paired with merely unlikely likelihood
Severe impact paired with merely possible likelihood
Moderate impact paired with near certain likelihood
questions.why: (3 x 5) + 3 = 18, compared with 15, 16 and 12.

questions.q: A High risk cannot be reduced with the resources available. What should happen next?
o: Lower the score until the activity fits the available resources
Proceed quietly and review the risk after the activity ends
Escalate in writing, propose a decision and record who decided
Mention it in a hallway chat and wait for instructions
questions.why: Escalation should be in writing, with a proposed decision and a record of who decided.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the risk assessment procedure?
o: Assign owners, identify risk, score, review, act, name who is at risk
Identify risk, name who is at risk, score, act, assign owners, review
Score the risk, identify who is at risk, review, act, assign owners
Act, identify risk, assign owners, score, name who is at risk, review
questions.why: The sequence is identify, who is at risk, score, act, owners and dates, review.

questions.q: Which practice makes a venue safer for children?
o: Visitors sign in and are never left alone with children
Visitors may enter freely when they carry a donor badge
Children choose any hidden room for private games after class
Staff keep one locked room for private talks with children
questions.why: Visitors must sign in and never be left alone with children.

questions.q: What should every partner agreement include?
o: Safeguarding clauses and the code of conduct, signed and briefed
Payment terms and the delivery schedule, signed, dated and filed
Branding rules and the logo placement, signed, dated and approved
Insurance cover and the vehicle details, signed, dated and stored
questions.why: Partners with access must sign safeguarding clauses and the code of conduct.

questions.q: Why is an unmonitored risk plan weak?
o: Written plans protect children even if nobody ever reads them
Donors always check each action before the whole activity starts
Incomplete action is an incomplete process and leaves risk open
Plans change automatically when staff leave their current team roles
questions.why: Plans that are not monitored leave the risks open.

questions.q: Who should help identify risks?
o: Only the board, because it signs the final risk register
Everyone, including participants and stakeholders, not just the safeguarding team
Only the safeguarding team, because it holds the formal training
Only external auditors, because they remain fully independent of staff
questions.why: Everyone helps identify risks, including participants.

questions.q: Why use a conditional offer?
o: It becomes final only when every check is back and clear
It prevents the person from reading the safeguarding policy too early
It reduces the salary until the first probation review finally ends
It lets the new person start unsupervised work while checks continue
questions.why: A conditional offer is final only when all checks are clear.

questions.q: Which reference practice is correct?
o: One reference from a friend who confirms the candidate's good character
Two references from relatives who confirm the candidate's home address details
A verbal reference from a current senior colleague of the candidate
Two references including the last employer, asked about conduct with children
questions.why: Use at least two references, including the last employer, and ask about conduct.

questions.q: When should induction take place?
o: Within probation but only after the first donor visit ends
Within 30 days and before any unsupervised contact with children
Within one year and after the first yearly appraisal meeting
Within 30 days but only for staff who meet children
questions.why: Induction is within 30 days and before unsupervised contact with children.

questions.q: Which is a recruitment mistake?
o: Keeping a checks tracker for every hire for easy later audit
Asking about employment gaps and why previous roles were ended early
Sharing the policy and code of conduct with candidates before interview
Giving a good reference to push out someone with proven misconduct
questions.why: References must be honest and include proven misconduct.

questions.q: Reports rise after training and new channels are set up. What does this usually mean?
o: Trust is rising, not that harm is increasing
Harm is rising so training should be stopped
Registers are faulty so reports should be removed
Staff are exaggerating so channels should be reduced
questions.why: Reports rising after training usually means trust is rising, not harm.

questions.q: Which barrier is a trust-in-the-mechanism problem?
o: People not knowing the channel exists or how to find it
A false sense of community and silence seen as being normal
Power distance, respect for authority and a fear of local stigma
Fear of retaliation and doubt that reports are ever acted on
questions.why: Fear of retaliation and doubt that reports are acted on are trust barriers.

questions.q: Which first step best improves reporting in an organisation?
o: Assess whether people know, trust and can reach the channels
Ask the employer to name which workers should report concerns
Buy a hotline number and print posters for all sites
Announce a zero tolerance rule and then wait for reports
questions.why: Assess first, then identify barriers, then act.

questions.q: Who should log every report, and when?
o: The board, in the annual report, after the yearly audit
Any manager, in a personal notebook, within the next week
The reporter, in the public log, at the next meeting
A named person, in the register, on the same day
questions.why: A named person should log every report in the register on the same day.

questions.q: A child says: 'Please do not tell anyone.' Which reply is best?
o: I promise to keep this secret forever between just you and me
I will go and speak to him first to hear his side
Thank you for telling me; I must tell someone who can help
Are you sure that is what happened? Please tell me every detail
questions.why: Never promise secrecy. Explain who you will tell and why.

questions.q: Who should lead an investigation into an allegation against a staff member?
o: The line manager who supervises the person who is accused
Any friendly colleague who knows the child and the family
The SFP/DSL acting alone as the main interviewer on site
Trained independent investigators who have no link to the case
questions.why: Investigators must be trained and independent, never the SFP/DSL alone.

questions.q: In triage, what comes first?
o: Check for immediate danger and act on safety first
Record the full story in writing before anything else
Inform the donor about the case before safety checks
Refer the person to legal services before danger checks
questions.why: Triage asks first whether anyone is in immediate danger.

questions.q: A girl needs medical care after a sexual assault in Lagos. Where should she be referred?
o: A vocational training skills centre, with her informed consent
A local education authority office, with her informed consent
A state legal aid office, with her informed consent
A sexual assault referral centre, with her informed consent
questions.why: Medical care after sexual assault is provided by sexual assault referral centres.

questions.q: A group photo is taken from behind with no names and the location shown only as Lagos. What is still needed before posting?
o: A longer caption naming the area to help donors
Informed consent and a safeguarding sign-off before any release
A staff member's personal account to post it faster
Nothing more because the faces are not visible there
questions.why: Consent and safeguarding sign-off are always needed.

questions.q: What is the triangle of risk in media use?
o: Face, name and location, which must never appear together
Name, school and class, which must never appear together
Location, date and time, which must never appear together
Face, age and gender, which must never appear together
questions.why: Face, name and location together lead someone straight to the child.

questions.q: A participant says beating a child worker teaches discipline. What does the behaviour change method suggest?
o: Validate the concern, then correct and offer a replacement
Ignore the view and move to the next slide
Remove the participant and report the view to police
Agree with the view and then add a warning
questions.why: Validate the thought, correct it, answer the fear and offer a replacement.

questions.q: What keeps an action plan alive?
o: Verbal promises, fixed dates, a board review and no backup
Shared ownership, open deadlines, a donor tracker and a deputy
Named owners, dates, a monthly tracker and a named backup
Strong intentions, flexible dates, a yearly review and a champion
questions.why: Owners, dates, monthly tracking and a backup keep the plan alive.
